title: Portuguese at Home
pronunciation_guide: English-friendly respelling for European Portuguese (Portugal), written once per phrase in tools/pt-pronunciation.json. CAPITALS mark the stressed syllable.

phrases.note: Levanta-te: the te ('yourself') goes after the verb with a hyphen, because in Portuguese you literally 'lift yourself' up.

phrases.pt: Está na hora de te levantares.
phrases.ph: sh-TAH nuh O-ruh duh tuh luh-vuhn-TAH-ruhsh
phrases.note: Está na hora de ... = It's time to ... Levantares has an extra -es because it's aimed at 'you'. Portuguese can add endings like that to the basic verb form.
Sai is the order form of sair (to leave). Da is de + a squashed together, so da cama = 'from the bed'.
Já is a tiny word that means 'now' or 'right away' here, but 'already' in other sentences. Parents use it a lot.
Vá lá is the everyday Portuguese 'come on'. You can use it to hurry someone, or to beg: 'Vá lá, mãe!'
Vais + a verb = 'you're going to ...', just like English. Chegar tarde = 'to arrive late'.
Atrasada means 'late' for a girl; for a boy it's atrasado. Here já means 'already'.
Acordar means 'to wake up', so acordada is 'awake' (a girl). A boy would be acordado.
Portugal uses the simple past dormiste ('you slept') here. 'Tens dormido' means 'have you been sleeping (lately)?', which is different.

phrases.en: What time did you go to sleep?
phrases.note: Adormecer means 'to fall asleep'. If you mean 'go to bed', say deitar-se: A que horas te deitaste?
Tomar banho ('take a bath') covers a shower or a bath. Já at the start works like 'yet' in the question.
Careful with the tone: shouted at someone who's annoying you, 'Vai tomar banho!' also means 'Get lost!'
From vestir-se (to dress yourself). Vestir also gives o vestido (a dress), so it's an easy one to remember.
Vestida is the girl form; a boy is vestido. Adding já makes it 'Are you dressed yet?'
Portuguese 'washes' teeth: lavar os dentes. Your toothbrush is a escova de dentes.
Pentear-se means to brush or comb your hair (o pente is a comb). The te comes before the verb because já is in front.
Tudo = everything. Don't mix it up with todo/toda, which means 'all' or 'whole' (o dia todo = the whole day).
Os teus sapatos is literally 'the your shoes'. In Portugal people normally keep that o/a/os/as before 'my' and 'your'.
O casaco covers both a coat and a jacket. A very warm winter coat can also be um sobretudo.
A mochila is a school rucksack. After não, the te jumps in front of the verb: não te esqueças, never não esqueças-te.
Esquecer-se de = to forget something. De + o becomes do, so it's do almoço (the lunch).
In Portugal a mobile phone is o telemóvel. Brazilians say celular, which sounds odd in Portugal.
A chave = key, as chaves = keys. Portuguese often says 'the keys' where English says 'your keys', because it's obvious whose.

phrases.en: What time do you need to leave?
phrases.pt: A que horas tens de sair?
phrases.ph: uh kuh O-ruhsh taynzh duh suh-EER
phrases.note: Ter de + a verb = 'to have to'. Tens de sair = 'you have to leave'. You'll also hear tens que sair, which means the same.

phrases.en: What time do you need to be there?
phrases.pt: A que horas tens de estar lá?
phrases.ph: uh kuh O-ruhsh taynzh duh sh-TAR lah
phrases.note: Lá means 'there', somewhere away from both of you. Aí is 'there' near the person you're talking to.
Pronta is for a girl — a boy says pronto. Don't confuse it with Spanish pronto (soon).
Quase = nearly or almost. Put it right before the word it changes: quase pronta, quase cinco horas.
Anda comes from andar (to walk), but Anda lá! is used to mean 'Come on, hurry!' To a group: Andem lá!
Despachar-se = to hurry up. You'll hear Despacha-te! every school morning in Portugal.
Ir embora means 'to go away' or 'to leave'. Temos de = we have to.
Word by word: 'I am at your wait'. You can also say Estou a esperar por ti — same meaning.
Estão todos = 'they're all'. Portuguese uses a plural verb here, while English says 'everyone is'.
Daqui a + a time = 'in ... from now'. Daqui a cinco minutos = five minutes from now.
Vamos embora means 'let's go' or 'we're off'. Adding já makes it 'right now'.
O carro is 'car' in Portuguese (coche is Spanish). No = em + o, so no carro = 'in the car'.
Bom dia is singular, unlike Spanish buenos días. Later on it's boa tarde (afternoon) and boa noite (evening/night).

phrases.pt: O teu despertador está a tocar.
phrases.ph: oo TAY-oo dush-puhr-tuh-DOR sh-TAH uh too-KAR
phrases.note: Está a tocar = 'is ringing' right now. Portugal uses estar a + verb for things happening now; Brazil says está tocando.
Ouviste = 'you heard', from ouvir (to hear). O despertador comes from despertar, 'to wake up'.
Voltar a + verb = 'to do something again'. Não voltes a adormecer = don't fall asleep again.

phrases.pt: A casa de banho está livre.
phrases.ph: uh KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo sh-TAH LEE-vruh
phrases.note: In Portugal the bathroom is a casa de banho ('house of bath'). Brazilians say banheiro.
Pequeno-almoço is literally 'little lunch' — Portugal's word for breakfast. Brazilians say café da manhã.

phrases.en: Have some breakfast before you go.
phrases.pt: Toma o pequeno-almoço antes de saíres.
phrases.ph: TO-muh oo puh-kay-nahl-MOH-soo AHN-tuzh duh suh-EE-ruhsh
phrases.note: Antes de saíres = 'before you leave'. After antes de, Portuguese uses the basic verb with an -es ending for 'you'.
Calçar is a special verb for putting on shoes and socks. Don't mix it up with as calças, which means trousers.
Vestir is used for putting on clothes like coats and jumpers. Põe o casaco is fine too.
A farda is the usual word for a uniform in Portugal. Most Portuguese state schools don't have one, but private schools often do.
Só mais = 'just more'. In Portuguese mais goes before the number: mais cinco minutos, mais um bocadinho.
Vai-te embora = 'take yourself away'. It's blunt: OK with family, rude to anyone else.
Daqui = de + aqui, 'from here'. So Sai daqui! is literally 'Leave from here!'
O quarto means 'bedroom'. It also means 'a quarter': um quarto de hora = fifteen minutes.
Cansada is for a girl — a boy says cansado. Use estou (not sou) because being tired doesn't last.
Word by word: 'I'm dead of sleepiness'. O sono = sleepiness. A boy says morto de sono.
Literally 'I've already got up!' The me sits before the verb because já comes first.
Estou a + verb = 'I'm doing it right now'. The me ('myself') is stuck onto the end with a hyphen.
Parar de + verb = 'to stop doing something'. Para de gritar! Para de mexer! (Stop fiddling!)
Portuguese skips the 'can': não encontro is literally 'I don't find'. That's how people normally say it.
A escova = brush. At home it usually means a hairbrush; a toothbrush is a escova de dentes.
Deixa-me em paz = 'leave me in peace'. Deixar means both 'to leave' and 'to let': Deixa-me ir! = Let me go!
Cedo = early, tarde = late. Demais ('too') goes after the word: cedo demais, frio demais.
Portuguese says 'I don't have hunger' — ter fome. Same pattern for thirsty: ter sede.
Já vou! is literally 'I'm already going!' — the standard shout back when someone calls you.
Apagar is used for lights and also means 'to rub out'. To switch a light on, say acender: Acende a luz!
Fechar = to close, abrir = to open. As cortinas is easy to remember because it's close to 'curtains'.
Não ... nada = 'not at all'. Portuguese is happy to use two negatives together, unlike English.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.note: À (with the accent) is a + a, 'to the'. So ir à escola = 'go to the school'.
Sinto-me = 'I feel', with me after the verb. If you mean you feel sick in your stomach, say Estou maldisposta (maldisposto for a boy).

phrases.pt: Está alguém na casa de banho!
phrases.ph: sh-TAH al-GAYN nuh KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo
phrases.note: Alguém = someone, ninguém = no one. Está alguém? is also what you ask when you knock.

phrases.en: He's been in there for ages!
phrases.pt: Ele está lá dentro há séculos!
phrases.ph: ayl sh-TAH lah DAYN-troo ah SEH-koo-loosh
phrases.note: Há + a time = 'for' something that's still going on. Portuguese keeps the verb in the present: ele está ... há séculos.

phrases.en: Who used all the hot water?
phrases.pt: Quem é que gastou a água quente toda?
phrases.ph: kayn eh kuh guhsh-TOH uh AH-gwuh kaynt TOH-duh
phrases.note: Quem é que ...? = 'Who ...?' Portuguese people often add é que after question words, and it doesn't change the meaning.

phrases.en: Can you take me in the car?
phrases.note: Levas-me? = 'Will you take me?' The me goes after the verb. De carro = 'by car' (de autocarro = by bus).
Monday is segunda-feira ('second day'). Most Portuguese weekdays are numbered: terça (Tue), quarta (Wed), quinta (Thu), sexta (Fri).
Na = em + a, so na casa de banho = 'in the bathroom'. Despacha-te! is the Portuguese 'Hurry up!'

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.note: Demorar = to take a long time. Ainda demoras muito? is literally 'Are you still taking long?'

phrases.pt: Os outros também precisam da casa de banho.
phrases.ph: oo-ZOH-troosh tahm-BAYN pruh-SEE-zown duh KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo
phrases.note: Precisar de = to need. The de joins with a to make da: precisam da casa de banho.
Literally 'You're not going out like that.' Assim = 'like this' or 'like that'. It's firm, so expect an argument!
Gira is a very Portuguese word for 'pretty' or 'nice' (giro for a boy). It also works for things: Que giro! = How cool!
Isso = 'that' (near the person you're talking to). Isto = 'this' (near you). Limpo = clean, sujo = dirty.
Desligar = to switch off a machine (ligar = switch on). For lights Portuguese uses apagar instead.
Baixar = to lower. To turn it up, say Aumenta a música or Põe a música mais alta.

phrases.en: You've been in there for ages.
phrases.pt: Estás aí dentro há imenso tempo.
phrases.ph: sh-TAHZ uh-EE DAYN-troo ah ee-MAYN-soo TAYM-poo
phrases.note: Imenso ('loads') is a favourite word in Portugal. Aí dentro = 'in there' where you are; lá dentro would be further away.
A porta = door. Watch out: o porto means a port, and Porto is also Portugal's second city.

phrases.en: Put a jumper on, it's cold.
phrases.pt: Veste uma camisola, que está frio.
phrases.ph: vesht OO-muh kuh-mee-ZO-luh, kuh sh-TAH FREE-oo
phrases.note: In Portugal a camisola is a jumper. In Brazil the same word means a nightie, so it's a funny mix-up.
A saia = skirt. Demasiado = 'too' and goes before the word. Curta ends in -a to match saia.
A maquilhagem is how Portugal spells makeup (Brazil: maquiagem). A mais after a word means 'too much'.

phrases.en: Don't leave your towel on the floor.
phrases.pt: Não deixes a toalha no chão.
phrases.ph: nown DAY-shuhz uh too-AH-lyuh noo shown
phrases.note: O chão = the floor or ground. 'Don't' orders with tu end in -es here: não deixes, não entres.
Literally 'Is that top mine?' A blusa covers most girls' tops. É minha = 'is mine'; for a masculine thing it's é meu.

phrases.en: Your clothes are on the chair.
phrases.pt: A tua roupa está na cadeira.
phrases.ph: uh TOO-uh RROH-puh sh-TAH nuh kuh-DAY-ruh
phrases.note: A roupa (clothes) is singular in Portuguese, so the verb is está, not estão.

phrases.en: It's still in the washing machine.
phrases.pt: Ainda está na máquina de lavar.
phrases.ph: uh-EEN-duh sh-TAH nuh MAH-kee-nuh duh luh-VAR
phrases.note: A máquina de lavar is the washing machine; the dishwasher is a máquina de lavar a loiça. Ainda = still.
Outra coisa = 'another thing', which is how Portuguese says 'something else'. No word for 'a' before outra.
Não ... mais = 'not any more'. Esperar means 'to wait' but also 'to hope', so context matters.
Ótima (ótimo for a boy) means 'great'. Portugal now spells it without the old p (óptimo).
Estou a + verb is the Portugal way to say you're doing it now. Brazilians would say estou me vestindo.
Tomar banho = to shower or bathe. Tomar also means 'to have' for food and drink: tomar o pequeno-almoço.
O duche is 'the shower' in Portugal. Brazilians say o chuveiro, which in Portugal is just the shower head.
Arranjar means 'to fix' or 'sort out'. O cabelo is the hair on your head; o pelo is body or animal hair.
Maquilhar-me = 'to make myself up'. The me hooks onto the end of the verb with a hyphen.
Portuguese says os dentes ('the teeth'), not 'my teeth' — with your own body, 'the' is enough.
Pronta is for a girl; a boy says Estou quase pronto. Quase = nearly.

phrases.en: I'll be ready in five minutes.
phrases.pt: Daqui a cinco minutos estou pronta.
phrases.ph: duh-KEE uh SEEN-koo mee-NOO-toosh sh-TOH PROHN-tuh
phrases.note: Portuguese often uses the present (estou) for something happening soon. A boy says pronto.
Só = 'just' or 'only'. You can also say Só um bocadinho ('just a little bit').
Dá-me = 'give me', with the me after the verb. Reuse it: Dá-me isso! (Give me that!)
Espera! is for one person. To a group, say Esperem! Espera aí! means 'Hang on!'
Vou já! means 'I'm coming right now!' It's a slightly more urgent version of Já vou!

phrases.en: I'll be there in a minute.
phrases.note: Num = em + um ('in a'). Estou aí = 'I'm there', used in Portuguese for 'I'll be there'.
Descer = to go down, subir = to go up. Já desço is short for 'I'm coming down now'.
English says 'are' but Portuguese says está, because a roupa (clothes) is one singular word.

phrases.pt: Onde está a minha sweat com capuz?
phrases.ph: ohnd sh-TAH uh MEE-nyuh sweht kohn kuh-POOSH
phrases.note: Portuguese kids borrow 'sweat' from English sweatshirt — and it's a minha sweat, a 'she' word. O capuz = hood.

phrases.pt: Viste as minhas calças de ganga?
phrases.ph: veesht uhzh MEE-nyuhsh KAL-suhzh duh GAHN-guh
phrases.note: In Portugal jeans are calças de ganga (ganga = denim). Viste? = 'Did you see?', used for 'Have you seen?'
Os meus = my (for more than one masculine thing). Os teus = your. Sapatos are shoes; trainers are sapatilhas.
Isto = 'this' for something you're holding when you don't name it. It never changes to match a/o.
Seco = dry, molhado = wet. The verb secar (to dry) gives you o secador, the hairdryer.
Podes ...? = Can you ...? It's the go-to way to ask a favour: Podes ajudar-me? Podes vir cá?
Precisar always needs de, and de + isto becomes disto. Para amanhã = 'for tomorrow'.
Sai is the order form of sair (to leave). Do = de + o, so do meu quarto = 'from my bedroom'.
Fecha = shut (to one person). To a group it's Fechem a porta. The same verb gives o fecho, a zip.
Entrar = to come in. A 'don't' order to one person changes the ending: entra → não entres.
Mudar de roupa = to change clothes. Just mudar-se means to move house, so keep de roupa in.

phrases.pt: Está alguém na casa de banho.
phrases.ph: sh-TAH al-GAYN nuh KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo
phrases.note: In Portugal it's está alguém ('someone is'). Brazilians would say tem alguém no banheiro.

phrases.en: Are you going to be long in the bathroom?
phrases.pt: Vais demorar muito na casa de banho?
phrases.ph: vyzh duh-moo-RAR MWEEN-too nuh KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo
phrases.note: Vais demorar muito? = 'Are you going to take long?' Handy for any queue: Vais demorar?
Há = 'there is' or 'there are'. Não há = there isn't. Brazilians often use tem instead.
The full name is o secador de cabelo ('hair dryer'), but at home everyone just says o secador.
Acabou-se = 'it's run out' (from acabar, to finish). Portugal spells it champô; Brazil writes xampu.
Higiénico has an é in Portugal; Brazil writes higiênico. Same word, different accent mark.

phrases.en: Does this look OK on me?
phrases.note: Ficar bem a alguém = to suit someone. Fica-me bem = 'it suits me', with me after the verb.
Não tenho nada = 'I haven't got anything'. Para vestir = 'to wear'. Reuse it: Não tenho nada para fazer.
Pronto ends in -o to match o pequeno-almoço, a 'he' word. Use estar (not ser) for 'ready'.
O almoço = lunch, o jantar = dinner, o lanche = afternoon snack. Almoçar means 'to have lunch'.
Jantar = dinner, the evening meal, and pronto = ready. O almoço is lunch and o pequeno-almoço is breakfast.
Pronta ends in -a because comida (food) is a feminine word. With o jantar you'd say pronto.
Vem = come! (the tu command of vir). Portuguese parents also shout Anda comer! — here anda just means 'come on'.
Vir buscar = come and get. It works for anything: Vem buscar a tua roupa (come and get your clothes).

phrases.en: What do you want for breakfast?
phrases.note: Pequeno-almoço (literally 'little lunch') is breakfast in Portugal. Brazilians say café da manhã.

phrases.en: What do you want for lunch?
phrases.note: Queres is the tu form of querer (to want). Portuguese usually drops the word tu because the -es ending already shows who.
In Portuguese you 'have' hunger: tens fome = literally 'do you have hunger?'. Thirst works the same: tens sede?

phrases.en: Do you want something to eat?
phrases.note: Alguma coisa = something (literally 'some thing'). Swap comer for beber and it means 'something to drink'.
Beber = to drink. Portuguese asks 'do you want to drink something?' rather than 'do you want a drink?'.

phrases.en: What do you want to drink?
phrases.note: O que = what, at the start of a question. Answer with Quero ... — Quero sumo means 'I want juice' (sumo is juice in Portugal).
No word for 'some' is needed: queres água? is simply 'want water?'. Remember the accent on the first a of água.
Mais = more. Short and handy: mais pão (more bread), mais água, mais um bocadinho (a tiny bit more).
Chega literally means 'does it arrive?', but here it's 'is that enough?'. Chega! on its own is a firm 'That's enough!'.
Já = already and acabaste = you finished. Portugal uses this simple past where English says 'have you finished?'.
False friend alert: come here is 'eat!', the tu command of comer. It has nothing to do with the English 'come'.
Provar = to try food (or try on clothes). Pelo menos = at least — a phrase you can use anywhere.
Bocadinho = a little bit, from bocado (a bit). Portuguese loves adding -inho to make things small or cute.
Nem sequer = not even. Provaste means 'you tried' — Portugal uses it where English says 'you haven't tried'.
After não, the command changes shape: come (eat!) becomes não comas (don't eat!).
Quase = nearly or almost. It's also a handy one-word answer to 'Is it ready?': Quase!

phrases.en: It'll be ready in ten minutes.
phrases.pt: Fica pronto daqui a dez minutos.
phrases.ph: FEE-kuh PROHN-too duh-KEE uh dezh mee-NOO-toosh
phrases.note: Daqui a = in (time from now): daqui a dez minutos is ten minutes from now. Don't use em for this.

phrases.en: Put your plate in the dishwasher.
phrases.pt: Põe o teu prato na máquina de lavar a loiça.
phrases.ph: poyn oo TAY-oo PRAH-too nuh MAH-kee-nuh duh luh-VAR uh LOY-suh
phrases.note: Máquina de lavar a loiça = dishwasher, literally 'machine for washing the dishes'. A loiça means plates, cups and bowls.
Lixo = rubbish, and o caixote do lixo is the bin itself. Põe is the tu command of pôr (to put).

phrases.en: Put it back in the fridge.
phrases.note: Voltar a + verb = do again, so volta a pô-lo = put it back. Frigorífico is 'fridge' in Portugal; Brazilians say geladeira.
Podes ...? = Can you ...? Pôr a mesa is 'set the table' — literally 'put the table'.
Levantar a mesa = clear the table (literally 'lift the table'). It's the opposite of pôr a mesa.

phrases.pt: Podes tirar a loiça da máquina?
phrases.ph: PO-duhsh tee-RAR uh LOY-suh duh MAH-kee-nuh
phrases.note: Tirar = take out. 'Take the dishes out of the machine' is how Portuguese families say 'empty the dishwasher'.

phrases.pt: Podes pôr a loiça na máquina?
phrases.ph: PO-duhsh pohr uh LOY-suh nuh MAH-kee-nuh
phrases.note: Pôr = put, the opposite of tirar (take out). Families say this rather than a special word for 'load'.
Deixar = to leave something somewhere. Isto aqui = 'this here' — isto is for things close to you.
Comeu = ate. O último = the last one; for a feminine thing like a bolacha (biscuit) it's a última.
Aí = there, near the person you're talking to; ali is further away. Não deixes is the 'don't' form of deixar.

phrases.en: Wash your hands before you eat.
phrases.pt: Lava as mãos antes de comer.
phrases.ph: LAH-vuh uhzh mownz AHN-tuzh duh koo-MAYR
phrases.note: Portuguese says 'wash the hands', not 'your hands' — with body parts, as mãos is enough.
Senta-te = sit (yourself) down. The te ('yourself') goes after the verb with a hyphen.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.note: Passas-me = will you pass me: the me goes after the verb with a hyphen. A quick, friendly way to ask.
Cuidado = careful. Quente means hot to touch; for spicy food Portuguese says picante.
Said before eating. The reply is Obrigado/Obrigada, or Igualmente, which means 'same to you'.

phrases.en: Don't eat with your mouth open.
phrases.note: De boca aberta = with your mouth open. Its opposite is de boca fechada (closed).
Telemóvel is a mobile in Portugal (celular in Brazil). Nada de ... = no ... at all, a handy way to ban something.
Há = there is/are, and ainda = still. Ainda há leite? = is there still some milk?
Ajudas-me = will you help me, with me after the verb. Portuguese often asks with a plain verb instead of 'can you'.
One word does the whole question: gostaste = did you like it? Answer Gostei! (I liked it) or Não gostei.

phrases.pt: O que há para o jantar?
phrases.ph: oo kuh ah PAH-ruh oo zhuhn-TAR
phrases.note: O que há para ...? = what is there for ...? Jantar is both 'dinner' and the verb 'to have dinner'.

phrases.pt: A que horas é o jantar?
phrases.ph: uh kuh O-ruhz eh oo zhuhn-TAR
phrases.note: A que horas = at what time. It works for anything: A que horas é o treino? (What time is training?)
Adding já (already) makes it 'is dinner ready yet?' — just the right impatient tone.
Vamos + verb = we're going to ... It's the easiest way to talk about what's about to happen.
Tenho fome = I'm hungry, literally 'I have hunger'. Never say estou fome.
Estou a morrer = I'm dying. Estar a + verb is how Portugal says 'doing right now'; Brazilians say estou morrendo.
Há = is there. The same word means 'there is' in normal sentences: Há bolo! (There's cake!)

phrases.en: Can I have something to eat?
phrases.note: Posso ...? = Can I ...? One of the most useful patterns: Posso ir? Posso ver?
Lanchar = to have a snack. O lanche is the afternoon snack Portuguese kids have after school.
Mais goes after the verb: comer mais = eat more. Swap in beber for 'drink more'.

phrases.pt: Podes fazer-me alguma coisa para comer?
phrases.ph: PO-duhsh fuh-ZAYR-muh al-GOO-muh KOY-zuh PAH-ruh koo-MAYR
phrases.note: Fazer-me = make me: the me goes after the verb with a hyphen. Para comer makes it clear you mean food.
Podemos ...? = Can we ...? It comes from poder. In Portugal pizza is sometimes also spelt piza.
Mandar vir comida is how Portugal says 'get a takeaway' — literally 'send for food to come'.
Ao = a + o, 'to the'. Portuguese puts o in front of the restaurant's name, just like ao cinema.
Gostar always needs de: de + isso joins to make disso. So 'I don't like that' is não gosto disso.
Quero = I want, from querer. Put não in front of the verb to make almost any sentence negative.
Literally 'I don't have hunger'. The same pattern gives não tenho sede (I'm not thirsty).
Just two words: já (already) + comi (I ate). Portugal uses this where English says 'I've eaten'.
Mais logo is a very Portuguese way to say 'later on today'. Como means 'I'll eat' here — the present often covers plans.

phrases.en: Can I eat in my room?
phrases.note: Quarto = bedroom (it also means 'quarter'). No = em + o, 'in the'.
Portuguese kids often just use the English word snacks. Onde estão = where are; for one thing it's onde está.
Batatas fritas means both crisps and chips. To be clear you mean crisps, say batatas fritas de pacote (from a packet).
Temos = we have. Portuguese turns it into a question just by raising your voice at the end.
A minha comida = my food. Portugal keeps the a ('the') before minha; Brazilians often drop it.
Estava a guardar = I was saving. Estar a + verb works in the past too (Brazilians say estava guardando).
Beber = to drink. Make it specific with Posso beber um copo de leite? — um copo is a glass.

phrases.en: Can you get me some water?
phrases.note: Ir buscar = go and get. Buscar-me = get for me, with the me after the verb and a hyphen.
Mesmo = really here. Use está bom for food that tastes good right now.
Cheia (full) is for a girl — a boy says cheio. Don't mix it up with estou farta, which means 'I'm fed up'.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.pt: Podes passar-me o sal, por favor?
phrases.ph: PO-duhsh puh-SAR-muh oo sal, poor fuh-VOR
phrases.note: Podes passar-me ...? = can you pass me ...? Swap in anything on the table: o pão, a água. Por favor = please.
Já não = not any more. So já não há leite = there's no milk left.
Uma torrada = a piece of toast. Pão is bread, and torrar means to toast.
Demais after a word means 'too': quente demais = too hot. Demasiado quente means the same.
Ajudar-te = help you: the te ('you') goes after the verb. Cozinhar is to cook; a cozinha is the kitchen.
Obrigada is what a girl says; a boy says obrigado. It matches the speaker, not the person being thanked.
Direita = straight, said to a girl; to a boy it's senta-te direito. The same word also means 'right' (direction).
Tirar = take off or away, and cotovelos = elbows. Da = de + a, 'off the'.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.pt: Não fales com a boca cheia.
phrases.ph: nown FAH-luhsh kohn uh BOH-kuh SHAY-uh
phrases.note: Boca cheia = full mouth. Não fales is the 'don't' form of falar (to speak).

phrases.pt: Usa a faca e o garfo.
phrases.ph: OO-zuh uh FAH-kuh ee oo GAR-foo
phrases.note: Faca = knife, garfo = fork, and colher = spoon. Usa is the tu command of usar (to use).

phrases.pt: Acaba o que tens no prato.
phrases.ph: uh-KAH-buh oo kuh taynzh noo PRAH-too
phrases.note: O que tens = what you have. Acaba is the tu command of acabar, to finish.
Está bom? = is it nice? about food. Bom becomes boa for feminine words: A sopa está boa?
Quem = who. It takes the he/she form quer, because 'who' is treated as one person.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the bread?
phrases.note: Pão is bread, and its plural is pães. In Portugal um pão usually means a single bread roll.
Parar de + verb = stop doing something: para de gritar, para de rir. Here para means 'stop', not 'for'.
Repetir means 'repeat', but at the table it means 'have seconds'. Kids can ask Posso repetir?
Terminar = to finish, just like acabar. Já terminaste? = are you finished (already)?
Acabarem = they finish. Portuguese can add -em to a basic verb like this to show it's 'they' doing it.
O garfo = the fork. Portuguese says 'the fork' where English says 'your fork'.
False friend: legumes means vegetables in general, not just beans and peas.
Pousem is the command to several people (vocês) from pousar, 'to put down' — said to the whole family at once.

phrases.pt: Para de brincar com a comida.
phrases.ph: PAH-ruh duh breen-KAR kohn uh koo-MEE-duh
phrases.note: Brincar = to play or mess about. Jogar is for sports and video games.
Esquisita means fussy about food (esquisito for a boy) — it doesn't mean 'exquisite'!

phrases.pt: Isto não tem nada de mal.
phrases.ph: EESH-too nown tayn NAH-duh duh mal
phrases.note: Não tem nada de mal = there's nothing wrong with it. Nada = nothing, mal = bad or wrong.
Refilar is very Portuguese for moaning or answering back. Não refiles! is a classic parent line.
Isto = this, for a thing or place, never a person. Restaurante is nearly the same as in English.
Here está is a command, 'keep', not 'is'. Quieta = still, for a girl; to a boy it's está quieto.

phrases.pt: Para de dar pontapés ao teu irmão.
phrases.ph: PAH-ruh duh dar pohn-tuh-PEHZ ow TAY-oo eer-MOWN
phrases.note: Dar pontapés = to kick, literally 'give kicks'. Ao teu irmão = to your brother.

phrases.en: Don't feed Monty under the table.
phrases.pt: Não dês comida ao Monty debaixo da mesa.
phrases.ph: nown daysh koo-MEE-duh ow MON-tee duh-BY-shoo duh MAY-zuh
phrases.note: In casual Portuguese names get o or a in front: ao Monty = to (the) Monty. Debaixo de = under.
Mastigar = to chew. De boca fechada = with your mouth closed — no word for 'your' needed.
Limpa = wipe or clean. Add ao guardanapo for 'on your napkin' — o guardanapo is a napkin.

phrases.en: Say thank you for the food.
phrases.note: Agradecer = to say thank you for something. One verb does the whole job of 'say thanks for'.
After não, the te jumps in front of the verb. Pede = ask for (pedir); perguntar is to ask a question.

phrases.pt: Levanta o teu prato, por favor.
phrases.ph: luh-VAHN-tuh oo TAY-oo PRAH-too, poor fuh-VOR
phrases.note: Levantar o prato = take your plate away from the table (literally 'lift your plate'), not 'eat it all up'.
Delicioso = delicious. For a feminine food, like a sopa (soup), it becomes deliciosa.
Sair = to leave or go out. Sair da mesa = leave the table (da = de + a).
Picante = spicy. Quente only means hot as in temperature, so don't use it for chilli.
Sobremesa is pudding or dessert — literally 'over the table', for what comes after the meal.

phrases.en: Can I have a bit less?
phrases.note: Pões-me = will you give me, literally 'put me'. Menos = less; the opposite is mais (more).
Disto = de + isto, for something right by you. For something near someone else it's disso.
Detestar = to hate, stronger than não gostar. Odeio isto also works but sounds very dramatic.
Nojento = disgusting. Blunt — fine with family, but rude to say about someone else's cooking.
Nojo = disgust. Que ...! = What a ...! — Que seca! (What a bore!) works the same way.

phrases.en: Why do we keep having this?
phrases.pt: Porque é que estamos sempre a comer isto?
phrases.ph: POOR-kuh eh kuh sh-TUH-moosh SAYM-pruh uh koo-MAYR EESH-too
phrases.note: Porque é que = why, the everyday European way to start. Estamos a comer = we're eating (estar a + verb).
Outra vez = again, literally 'another time'. Outra vez?! on its own is a moany 'Again?!'.
Mais um bocado = a bit more. Um bocado means 'a bit' or 'a piece' of something.
Adding já makes it 'I'm full now'. Cheia is for a girl; a boy says cheio.
Levantar-se = to get up. After já, the me jumps in front of the verb: já me posso levantar.
Frio = cold. Está (not é) is used because it's cold right now, not always.
O que é isto? = what is this? Swap isto for aquilo for something over there.
Que bom! = Yum! or How nice! It works for good news too, not just food.
Dás-me = will you give me, from dar (to give). Quick and friendly, but adding por favor never hurts.
Diz-lhe = tell him: lhe means 'to him' (or 'to her') and goes after the verb with a hyphen.
Imitar = to copy someone's actions; copiar is more for copying work. Está a imitar = is copying right now.

phrases.pt: Ele tem mais do que eu!
phrases.ph: ayl tayn mysh doo kuh AY-oo
phrases.note: Mais do que = more than, and ele tem = he has. Menos do que is 'less than'.
False friend: justo means fair, not 'just'. Que injustiça! is another way to complain.
Vegetariana is for a girl — a boy says vegetariano. Sou (from ser) is for what you are, not how you feel.

phrases.en: Do I have to eat all of it?
phrases.note: Tenho de = I have to. In Portugal people say tenho de; Brazilians usually say tenho que.
Bocadinho = a little bit: bocado (a piece) plus -inho, the 'little' ending. Very Portuguese.
A sobremesa = pudding or dessert, literally 'over the table' (sobre + mesa).

phrases.en: Can I have it with nothing on it?
phrases.pt: Pode ser sem nada por cima?
phrases.ph: pod ser sayn NAH-duh poor SEE-muh
phrases.note: Pode ser...? = 'Can it be...?' — a polite way to ask for food a certain way. Sem nada por cima = with nothing on top.
Correu comes from correr (to run), but Como correu? means 'How did it go?' Use it for tests, days and trips.
O teu dia: in Portugal 'your' usually has o or a in front — o teu dia, a tua mochila.
Fizeste = you did, from fazer. Portuguese uses this one past form where English says 'did' or 'have done'.
Alguma coisa = anything or something, word for word 'some thing'. Aconteceu = happened.
TPC stands for trabalhos para casa — homework. Portuguese kids say TPC all the time.

phrases.pt: Já fizeste os trabalhos de casa?
phrases.ph: zhah fee-ZESHT oosh truh-BAH-lyoozh duh KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Já = already. Portuguese adds já where English says 'Have you done it yet?'
Para quando? = 'for when?' — the everyday way to ask about a deadline. Answer: É para amanhã.
O means 'it' here. It sits before acabaste because já pulls it forward; without já you'd say Acabaste-o?
Precisar de = to need. Portuguese always needs the de: precisas de ajuda, preciso de dinheiro.

phrases.en: Have you got a test tomorrow?
phrases.note: Um teste is a normal school test. Um exame is a bigger official exam, like the national ones in year 9.
There's no separate word for 'revise' — Portuguese just says estudar (to study).

phrases.en: What lesson have you got first?
phrases.note: Uma aula = a lesson; a sala de aula is the classroom. Don't mix it up with a escola (the school).
A que horas...? = At what time...? Swap the verb to ask about anything: A que horas começas? (start).
Ir buscar = to pick someone up, literally 'go and fetch'. Que te vá buscar = 'that I go and fetch you'.

phrases.en: Where should I pick you up?
phrases.note: Te ('you') comes before vou because onde (where) is a question word, and question words pull it forward.

phrases.en: What time should I pick you up?
phrases.pt: A que horas te vou buscar?
phrases.ph: uh kuh O-ruhsh tuh voh boosh-KAR
phrases.note: Vou buscar-te = I'll pick you up. In a question starting A que horas, the te jumps in front: te vou buscar.
Manda-me mensagem = send me a message. Acabares is the form used after quando for something still to come.

phrases.en: Let me know when you're ready.
phrases.note: Pronta is for a girl — a boy is pronto. Avisar = to let someone know, so avisa-me = let me know.

phrases.pt: Não te esqueças do equipamento de Educação Física.
phrases.ph: nown tuh sh-KEH-suhzh doo ee-kee-puh-MAYN-too duh ee-doo-kuh-SOWN FEE-zee-kuh
phrases.note: Educação Física (EF) = PE, and your kit is o equipamento. After não, the te comes before the verb.
Fazer a mochila = to pack your bag, literally 'make the backpack'. For a suitcase: fazer a mala.

phrases.en: Do you need anything for tomorrow?
phrases.pt: Precisas de alguma coisa para amanhã?
phrases.ph: pruh-SEE-zuhzh duh al-GOO-muh KOY-zuh PAH-ruh ah-muh-NYAHN
phrases.note: Amanhã = tomorrow, but a manhã = the morning. So amanhã de manhã = tomorrow morning.

phrases.pt: Primeiro faz os trabalhos de casa.
phrases.ph: pree-MAY-roo fash oosh truh-BAH-lyoozh duh KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Faz is the command 'do!' when talking to one person, from fazer. Primeiro = first.

phrases.en: What have you got to do?
phrases.pt: O que é que tens de fazer?
phrases.ph: oo kyeh kuh taynzh duh fuh-ZER
phrases.note: O que é que...? is a very Portuguese way to ask 'What...?' The é que adds no meaning — it just sounds natural.
Como correu? = how did it go? Reply Correu bem (it went well) or Correu mal (it went badly).
Uma nota = a mark. Up to year 9, Portuguese marks go 1–5 (5 is best); older kids get 0–20, and 10 is a pass.
Muito bem = well done, word for word 'very well'. Make it bigger with Muito bem, parabéns! (congratulations).

phrases.en: Who did you have lunch with?
phrases.note: Almoçar is one verb meaning 'to have lunch'. Same idea: jantar (have dinner), lanchar (have an afternoon snack).
As tuas amigas = your friends who are girls. For boys or a mixed group, say os teus amigos.
Mostrar = to show. In a command, the me ('me') goes after the verb with a hyphen: mostra-me.

phrases.en: Put your books in your bag.
phrases.note: Põe = put! (from pôr). Na is em + a, 'in the' — Portuguese glues the two words together.

phrases.en: Don't leave it till the last minute.
phrases.pt: Não deixes para a última hora.
phrases.ph: nown DAY-shuhsh PAH-ruh uh OOL-tee-muh O-ruh
phrases.note: Última hora = last minute, literally 'last hour'. Não deixes = don't leave — 'don't' changes deixa to deixes.
No word for 'any' is needed: Não tenho TPC = I don't have (any) homework.
Já fiz = I've already done it. Portuguese often drops the 'it' when everyone knows what you mean.
Mais logo = later today. Portuguese often uses the present faço (I do) to mean 'I'll do'.

phrases.en: I need help with my homework.
phrases.pt: Preciso de ajuda com os TPC.
phrases.ph: pruh-SEE-zoo duh uh-ZHOO-duh kohn oosh tay-pay-SAY
phrases.note: TPC doesn't change when it means lots of homework: os TPC. Preciso de = I need.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Podes ...? = Can you ...? — a pattern for asking anything. In ajudar-me, the me hooks on with a hyphen.
Perceber = to understand in Portugal (Brazilians prefer entender). Não percebo nada = I don't get it at all.
Isto = this (near me); isso = that (near you). Ver means 'to look at' as well as 'to see'.
Uma coisa = something, literally 'a thing'. Imprimir = to print; the printer is a impressora.

phrases.pt: A impressora não está a funcionar.
phrases.ph: uh eem-pruh-SOH-ruh nown sh-TAH uh foon-syoo-NAR
phrases.note: Não está a funcionar = isn't working right now. Estar a + verb is the Portugal way to say '-ing'.

phrases.en: I need something for school tomorrow.
phrases.pt: Preciso de uma coisa para a escola amanhã.
phrases.ph: pruh-SEE-zoo duh OO-muh KOY-zuh PAH-ruh uh sh-KO-luh ah-muh-NYAHN
phrases.note: Para a escola = for school. Portuguese keeps the a ('the') where English just says 'school'.
Esquecer-se = to forget, and the me after the hyphen is part of the verb. Esqueci-me! is the classic excuse.

phrases.pt: Preciso de dinheiro para a escola.
phrases.ph: pruh-SEE-zoo duh dee-NYAY-roo PAH-ruh uh sh-KO-luh
phrases.note: O dinheiro = money. Useful add-on: para a visita de estudo (for the school trip).

phrases.en: I need you to sign this.
phrases.note: Assinar = to sign. After preciso que ('I need you to'), assinas changes to assines.
No 'a' needed: tenho teste. Depois de amanhã = the day after tomorrow.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.note: À = a + a ('to the'), marked with a backwards accent. Ir à escola = to go to school.
Cansada is for a girl — a boy says cansado. Use estou, not sou, for how you feel right now.
Uma seca = a bore, literally 'a drought'. Que seca! = How boring! — very Portuguese.
Correu bem = it went fine. The short answer kids give to end the conversation.
Portuguese uses two negatives: não ... nada = nothing, word for word 'not happened nothing'.
Sei comes from saber, to know facts. For knowing a person you'd use conhecer.
Lembrar-se = to remember. After não, the me moves in front of the verb: não me lembro.
Fizemos = we did, from fazer. Again não ... nada: Portuguese needs both negatives.
Vir buscar = come and pick up. You say vir (come) because the parent is coming to you.

phrases.en: Can you pick me up early?
phrases.note: Mais cedo = earlier. Cedo = early and tarde = late — tarde also means afternoon.

phrases.en: What time are you picking me up?
phrases.pt: A que horas me vens buscar?
phrases.ph: uh kuh O-ruhzh muh vaynzh boosh-KAR
phrases.note: Vens = you come, from vir. The me sits before vens because the sentence is a question.
Portuguese has no neat 'test me', so kids say fazer perguntas, 'ask questions'. Uma pergunta = a question.
É para amanhã = it's due tomorrow, literally 'it's for tomorrow'. Para marks the deadline.
Tive = I got (from ter). In Portugal a boa nota is a 4 or 5 out of 5, or about 16+ out of 20.
Passar = to pass a test or a school year. The opposite is chumbar (to fail).
Chumbar = to fail. It's also used for repeating a school year: ele chumbou o ano.
Portuguese uses estudar for both 'study' and 'revise'. Tenho de = I have to.
Posso ...? = Can I ...? Spanish says ordenador, but Portuguese says o computador, close to English.
Ficar de castigo = to get a detention or be punished, literally 'stay on punishment'. Parents say Estás de castigo!

phrases.pt: Vamos ter uma visita de estudo.
phrases.ph: VUH-moosh ter OO-muh vee-ZEE-tuh duh sh-TOO-doo
phrases.note: Uma visita de estudo = a school trip, literally 'a study visit'. Vamos ter = we're going to have.
O quarto = bedroom (not 'quarter'). Vai + verb = go and do something: vai arrumar = go and tidy.

phrases.pt: O teu quarto está uma desarrumação!
phrases.ph: oo tew KWAR-too sh-TAH OO-muh duh-zuh-rroo-muh-SOWN
phrases.note: Desarrumação = mess: des- (un-) plus arrumação (tidiness). Arrumado = tidy, desarrumado = messy.
Arrumaste = you tidied, from arrumar. With já at the front it means 'Have you ... yet?'
Apanhar = to pick up from the floor. It also means to catch: apanhar o autocarro (catch the bus).
Arrumar means 'put away' as well as 'tidy', so arruma isso = put that away.
A roupa = clothes. It's one singular word in Portuguese, even though English 'clothes' is plural.

phrases.en: Put your dirty clothes in the wash.
phrases.pt: Põe a roupa suja para lavar.
phrases.ph: poyn uh RROH-puh SOO-zhuh PAH-ruh luh-VAR
phrases.note: Suja = dirty; it ends in -a to match a roupa. Para lavar = to be washed.
Limpo = clean, sujo = dirty. They end in -o because isso ('that') counts as masculine.

phrases.en: Don't leave it on the floor.
phrases.note: O chão = the floor. The o here means 'it', and after não it goes in front of the verb.
Fazer a cama = to make the bed, just like English. Faz = make! to one person.
Abre = open! Abrir works for curtains, doors, windows and even apps: abre a app.
A janela = window. It looks like janeiro (January) but has nothing to do with it.
Fechar = to close. You'll see fechado (closed) on shop doors in Portugal.
A porta = the door. Handy extra: Fecha a porta à chave = lock the door (close it with the key).
Deixar = to leave something somewhere. Aberta = open, ending in -a to match a porta.
Apagar = to turn off a light. It also means to delete or rub out: apaga isso.
Acender = to switch on a light or light a fire. For a TV or computer, say liga: liga a televisão.

phrases.pt: Podes trazer isso cá para baixo?
phrases.ph: PO-dsh truh-ZER EE-soo kah PAH-ruh BY-shoo
phrases.note: Trazer = to bring, towards the speaker. Cá para baixo = down here.

phrases.pt: Podes levar isto lá para cima?
phrases.ph: PO-dzh luh-VAR EESH-too lah PAH-ruh SEE-muh
phrases.note: Levar = to take, away from you — the opposite of trazer. Lá para cima = up there.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Ajudar = to help. Shout Ajuda! on its own and it means 'Help!'
Mãozinha = a little hand, from mão plus -zinha. Dá-me = give me, with the me after a hyphen.
De quem? = whose?, literally 'of who?'. The answer could be É meu (it's mine).
Teu = yours, to one person. For a feminine thing it changes: A camisola é tua?
Onde se põe? = where does it go?, literally 'where is it put?'. The se makes it general, not about anyone.
Aspirar = to hoover — just one verb. The hoover itself is o aspirador.
Mudar = to change. Os lençóis = the sheets; just one is um lençol.
Pendurar = to hang up. A toalha = towel, and a toalha de mesa is a tablecloth.

phrases.pt: Leva o lixo lá para fora.
phrases.ph: LEH-vuh oo LEE-shoo lah PAH-ruh FO-ruh
phrases.note: O lixo = the rubbish or the bin. Lá para fora = out there, outside.

phrases.en: Can you hang the washing out?
phrases.note: Estender a roupa = hang the washing out, literally 'spread out the clothes'. Portuguese balconies are full of it.
O estendal = the washing line or clothes airer. Apanhar a roupa = bring the washing in.
Dobrar = to fold. It also means to dub a film: um filme dobrado.
Cheirar mal = to smell bad; cheirar bem = to smell nice. Cheira a queimado = it smells burnt.

phrases.en: There are dirty cups in your room.
phrases.pt: Há chávenas sujas no teu quarto.
phrases.ph: ah SHAH-vuh-nuhsh SOO-zhuhsh noo tew KWAR-too
phrases.note: Há = there is/there are. Uma chávena = a cup in Portugal; Brazilians say xícara. A mug is uma caneca.
A vez = a turn. É a tua vez = it's your turn.
Ontem = yesterday. Fiz = I did, from fazer — the same word for 'I did' and 'I made'.
Está bem also works on its own as 'OK'. O meu quarto: in Portugal 'my' usually has o or a in front.

phrases.pt: Para de entrar no meu quarto!
phrases.ph: PAH-ruh duh ayn-TRAR noo mew KWAR-too
phrases.note: Parar de + verb = stop doing something. Para com isso! = Stop it!
Mexer em = to touch or mess with. Não mexas! is what you shout at a brother or sister.
Disto = de + isto, 'of this', so depois disto = after this. Faço here means 'I'll do it'.

phrases.pt: Porque é que sou sempre eu?
phrases.note: Porque é que...? = Why...? Sempre eu = always me — the classic complaint.
Arrumei = I tidied, from arrumar. Já turns it into 'I've already tidied!'
O aspirador = the hoover. In Brazil it's usually o aspirador de pó (dust hoover).

phrases.en: It's his turn to empty the dishwasher.
phrases.pt: É a vez dele de esvaziar a máquina da loiça.
phrases.ph: eh uh vezh DAY-luh duh zh-vuh-ZYAR uh MAH-kee-nuh duh LOY-suh
phrases.note: A máquina da loiça = the dishwasher, short for máquina de lavar a loiça. Dele = his.
Unlike Spanish me gusta, Portuguese says gosto (I like). Before a thing it adds de: gosto de pizza.
Tudo = everything. Starting with eu (I) adds a bit of attitude: 'I know where it all is'.
Bater à porta = to knock at the door; bater on its own means to hit.
Não me arrumes: the me ('for me') goes before the verb after não, and arrumas changes to arrumes.

phrases.en: Where did you put my hoodie?
phrases.note: A sweat = a sweatshirt or hoodie in Portugal, borrowed from English. A hood is o capuz.
Encontrar = to find. Não ... nada = nothing, with both negatives.
Já vou = I'm coming, literally 'already I go'. Kids often shorten está bem to 'tá bem.
Sujo is for masculine things like o casaco. For a feminine one, like a camisola: não está suja.
Fazer a cama = to make the bed. Starting with já shows it's done already.

phrases.en: Why do I have to do everything?
phrases.pt: Porque é que tenho de fazer tudo eu?
phrases.ph: poor-KEH-kuh TAY-nyoo duh fuh-ZER TOO-doo AY-oo
phrases.note: Putting eu (me) at the very end stresses it: 'why do I have to do everything, me?'
Quer dizer = means, literally 'wants to say'. Mais logo (later) is what kids say to put jobs off.

phrases.en: I don't care whose it is.
phrases.pt: Não me interessa de quem é.
phrases.ph: nown muh een-tuh-REH-suh duh kayn eh
phrases.note: Não me interessa = I don't care, literally 'it doesn't interest me'. Blunt — fine at home, rude elsewhere.
Desculpa = sorry, but desculpas also means excuses. Sem = without.
Tanto faz is the Portuguese 'whatever'. Digas comes from dizer (to say) — it's the form used after não: não digas = don't say.

phrases.en: Don't roll your eyes at me.
phrases.note: Revirar os olhos = to roll your eyes. After não, the me ('at me') moves in front of the verb.
Porque = because, but Porquê? on its own = why? Porque eu disse (literally 'because I said') is the classic parent full stop.

phrases.en: You said that an hour ago.
phrases.note: Há uma hora = an hour ago. Há (literally 'there is') + a time works like 'ago': há dois dias = two days ago.
Voltar a + verb means 'to do again': não volto a pedir = I won't ask again. Volto a dizer = I'll say it again.
Responder torto = to answer back rudely (torto means 'crooked'). Plain não me respondas also works.
Vou + verb = 'I'm going to': vou contar = I'm going to count. Até means 'up to' or 'until'.

phrases.pt: Daqui a um minuto, não — agora.
phrases.ph: duh-KEE uh oon mee-NOO-too, nown uh-GO-ruh
phrases.note: Daqui a = in (a time from now): daqui a um minuto = in a minute, daqui a uma hora = in an hour. Agora = now.

phrases.en: You're not busy, you're on your phone.
phrases.pt: Não estás ocupada, estás agarrada ao telemóvel.
phrases.ph: nown sh-TAHZ o-koo-PAH-duh, sh-TAHZ uh-guh-RRAH-duh ow tuh-luh-MO-vel
phrases.note: Agarrada ao telemóvel = glued to your phone (agarrar = to grab). A boy is ocupado and agarrado. Brazilians say celular.

phrases.en: I don't care who did it.
phrases.note: Quem foi? = who did it? (literally 'who was it?'). Não me interessa = it doesn't interest me — firm but not rude.

phrases.en: If you know, why haven't you done it?
phrases.pt: Se sabes, porque é que não o fizeste?
phrases.ph: suh SAH-buhsh, poor-KEH-kuh nown oo fee-ZESHT
phrases.note: Porque é que...? is the everyday way to ask 'why...?' in Portugal. Fizeste = you did, from fazer (to do).

phrases.pt: Então porque é que não está feito?
phrases.note: Feito means 'done' (from fazer). Está feito = it's done; já está feito = it's already done.
Tentativa = attempt (from tentar, to try). It's boa, not bom, because tentativa is a feminine word. Best said with a raised eyebrow.
Bufar = to huff and puff. Para de + verb = stop doing something: para de gritar = stop shouting.
Essa ('that one') means the excuse. Putting it first adds weight — like saying 'that one, I already know'.
Literally 'don't come to me with that one'. Venhas is from vir (to come), in the form used after não for commands.
Arranjar desculpas = to make excuses (arranjar = to find or sort out). Desculpa on its own means 'sorry'.
Mais logo = later today — a very Portuguese phrase. Faço ('I do') stands in for 'I'll do', as the present often does.

phrases.en: I'll do it in a minute.
phrases.note: Daqui a bocado = in a bit (bocado means 'a piece'). The go-to Portuguese way to put a job off.

phrases.en: I was going to do it!
phrases.note: Ia = I was going to (from ir, to go). Ia + any verb describes a plan: ia sair = I was going to go out.
Já means 'already', so já sei is 'I know already' — it sounds a bit impatient, which is exactly the point.
Disseste = you told (from dizer). The me goes before the verb because já comes first in the sentence.
Ouvi-te = I heard you: te ('you') is joined on after the verb with a hyphen, as usual in Portugal.
Estar a + verb means doing it right now: estou a fazer. Brazilians say estou fazendo instead.
Espera is 'wait' to one person; to several people say esperem. Esperar can also mean 'to hope'.
Espera aí = hang on (literally 'wait there'). The aí just softens it, and you'll hear it all the time.
Só = just/only. Kids also say só um bocadinho — 'just a little bit' — to buy time.
Porquê? with an accent is 'why?' said on its own or at the end. Inside a longer question use porque é que...?

phrases.en: Why do I have to do it?
phrases.pt: Porque é que tenho de ser eu a fazer?
phrases.ph: poor-KEH-kuh TAY-nyoo duh ser AY-oo uh fuh-ZER
phrases.note: Tenho de = I have to. Ser eu a fazer ('be me doing it') stresses 'why ME?'. Brazilians tend to say tenho que.

phrases.pt: Porque é que não é ele a fazer?
phrases.ph: poor-KEH-kuh nown eh AY-luh uh fuh-ZER
phrases.note: Não é ele a fazer = 'it isn't him doing it' — Portuguese uses é ... a + verb to point at who should do a job.
Meu = mine for masculine things. For a feminine one, like a camisola, say não é minha.
Fiz = I did (from fazer). Starting with eu stresses 'I didn't — someone else did'.
Não fui eu = it wasn't me (literally 'I wasn't'). The standard reply whenever something gets broken.

phrases.pt: Não fui eu que deixei isso aí.
phrases.ph: nown fwee AY-oo kuh day-SHAY EE-soo uh-EE
phrases.note: Deixar = to leave something somewhere. Aí means 'there, near you'; ali is 'over there'.
Arrumar = to tidy up. You'll hear the command form a lot: arruma o quarto! = tidy your room!

phrases.pt: O meu quarto não está assim tão mal.
phrases.ph: oo mew KWAR-too nown sh-TAH uh-SEEN town mal
phrases.note: Assim tão = 'that' in 'not that bad'. Notice o meu quarto: Portugal keeps o ('the') before 'my'.
O ('it') sits before encontro because of não. For a feminine thing, like a mochila, say não a encontro.
Ficar here means 'to belong / be kept'. Onde é que...? is the chatty way to ask 'where...?'.

phrases.en: What do you want me to do?
phrases.pt: O que é que queres que eu faça?
phrases.ph: oo kyeh kuh KEH-ruhsh kuh AY-oo FAH-suh
phrases.note: After queres que ('you want that'), fazer changes to faça — a special verb form used for wishes and orders.
Mesmo = really. Tenho mesmo de...? = do I really have to...? — the classic moan.
Ontem = yesterday, hoje = today, amanhã = tomorrow. Fiz = I did.
A vez = the turn. A vez dele = his turn (dele = 'of him'); a vez dela = her turn.
Vez also means 'time' as in how often: uma vez = once, duas vezes = twice. A minha vez = my turn.
Sou sempre eu = it's always me. Sempre = always and nunca = never — both handy in an argument.
Ocupada is for a girl — a boy says ocupado. Estou (from estar) describes how you are right now.
Acabei = I finished (from acabar). Portuguese adds já ('already') where English says 'I've'.
Limpo = clean for a masculine thing like o quarto; use limpa for a feminine one like a cozinha.
Posso...? = Can I...? Swap the verb for loads of requests: posso sair? posso ver televisão?

phrases.en: What do I get for it?
phrases.pt: E o que é que eu ganho com isso?
phrases.ph: ee oo kyeh kuh AY-oo GUH-nyoo kohn EE-soo
phrases.note: Ganhar = to win or earn. O que é que eu ganho? is a cheeky 'what's in it for me?'.
A culpa = fault or blame. Minha comes after the word here and is feminine to match culpa.
Pousar = to put down. O telemóvel is 'phone' in Portugal — Brazilians say celular.
Largar = to let go of. Larga is firmer than pousa — larga isso! means 'drop that!'.

phrases.en: How long have you been on your phone?
phrases.pt: Há quanto tempo estás no telemóvel?
phrases.ph: ah KWAHN-too TAYN-poo sh-TAHZH noo tuh-luh-MO-vel
phrases.note: Há quanto tempo...? = how long have you been...? Portuguese uses estás ('you are') here, not a past form.
Baixar = to lower or turn down. It comes from baixo, which means 'low' (and also 'short').
Isso = that (near you). Baixa isso works for music, the TV, a game — anything loud.
Alto means 'loud' here, though it also means 'tall'. Demasiado = too (much).
Os auscultadores = headphones in Portugal; Brazilians say fones de ouvido. Põe = put (on), from pôr.
O som = the sound. Baixa o som = turn the volume down — works for the TV, a phone or a speaker.

phrases.pt: O que é que estás a ver?
phrases.ph: oo kyeh kuh sh-TAHZ uh ver
phrases.note: Estás a ver = you're watching right now (estar a + verb). Ver means both 'to see' and 'to watch'.

phrases.pt: A que é que estás a jogar?
phrases.ph: uh kyeh kuh sh-TAHZ uh zhoo-GAR
phrases.note: Jogar a = to play a game: jogar à bola, jogar a Minecraft. For instruments Portuguese uses tocar.

phrases.pt: Com quem é que estás a falar?
phrases.ph: kohn kayn eh kuh sh-TAHZ uh fuh-LAR
phrases.note: Portuguese says 'talk with', not 'talk to': falar com alguém. So 'who to?' becomes com quem? ('with whom?').
Ainda = still. Ainda estás...? = are you still...? — try ainda estás na cama? (still in bed?).
Carregar = to charge a battery, but also 'to carry' or 'to press': carrega no botão = press the button.
O carregador = the charger, from carregar (to charge). O teu = your — with o ('the') in front, as Portugal does.

phrases.en: Don't forget to charge your phone.
phrases.pt: Não te esqueças de carregar o telemóvel.
phrases.ph: nown tuh sh-KEH-suhzh duh kuh-rruh-GAR oo tuh-luh-MO-vel
phrases.note: Não te esqueças de... = don't forget to... The te goes before the verb because of não.

phrases.pt: Já tiveste tempo de ecrã que chegue.
phrases.ph: zhah tee-VESHT TAYN-poo duh ay-KRAHN kuh shayg
phrases.note: O ecrã = screen in Portugal (Brazil says tela). Que chegue = 'enough', from chegar — já chega! means 'that's enough!'.
Está na hora de... = it's time to... Desligar = to switch off; ligar = to switch on.

phrases.pt: Mais cinco minutos e depois desligas.
phrases.ph: mysh SEEN-koo mee-NOO-toozh ee duh-POYZH dzh-LEE-guhsh
phrases.note: Desligas literally means 'you switch off' — Portuguese often uses this plain form as a calm order.

phrases.en: No, I'm not extending your time limit.
phrases.pt: Não, não te vou dar mais tempo.
phrases.ph: nown, nown tuh voh dar mysh TAYN-poo
phrases.note: Não te vou dar = I'm not going to give you. After não, te ('you') jumps in front of vou.

phrases.en: Why do you need more time?
phrases.pt: Porque é que precisas de mais tempo?
phrases.note: Precisar de = to need. Portuguese always adds de: preciso de ajuda = I need help.
Descansar = to rest. Portuguese says os olhos ('the eyes'), not 'your eyes', when it's obvious whose.
Desliga = switch off. Its opposite liga also means 'ring': liga-me = call me.
O comando = the remote in Portugal; Brazilians say o controle remoto.

phrases.pt: A quem é que estás a mandar mensagens?
phrases.ph: uh kayn eh kuh sh-TAHZ uh mahn-DAR muh-SAH-zhaynsh
phrases.note: Mandar mensagens = to send messages. Mandar also means 'to be in charge': quem manda aqui sou eu!
O computador = the computer. Spain says ordenador, but Portugal says computador.

phrases.pt: Hoje à noite deixa o telemóvel lá em baixo.
phrases.ph: ohzh ah noyt DAY-shuh oo tuh-luh-MO-vel lah ayn BY-shoo
phrases.note: Lá em baixo = downstairs (literally 'down there'); lá em cima = upstairs. Hoje à noite = tonight.

phrases.en: Can you turn it up a bit?
phrases.pt: Podes aumentar um bocadinho o som?
phrases.ph: PO-dzh ow-mayn-TAR oon boo-kuh-DEE-nyoo oo sohn
phrases.note: Podes...? = Can you...? Aumentar = to turn up or increase. Um bocadinho ('a little bit') is everywhere in Portugal.
Partilhar = to share in Portugal (Brazilians say compartilhar). Partilhes is the form used after não in orders.

phrases.en: Look at me, not your phone.
phrases.pt: Olha para mim, não para o telemóvel.
phrases.ph: O-lyuh PAH-ruh meen, nown PAH-ruh oo tuh-luh-MO-vel
phrases.note: Olhar para = to look at. Portuguese needs the para: olha para mim = look at me.
O meu telemóvel = my phone. In Portugal o ('the') stays before meu; Brazilians often drop it.
Viste? = did you see? Portugal uses this simple past where English says 'have you seen'.

phrases.pt: Podes ligar para o meu telemóvel?
phrases.ph: PO-dzh lee-GAR PAH-ruh oo mew tuh-luh-MO-vel
phrases.note: Ligar para = to ring or call someone. Liga-me! = ring me! The same verb also means 'to switch on'.

phrases.pt: O meu telemóvel ficou sem bateria.
phrases.ph: oo mew tuh-luh-MO-vel fee-KOH sayn buh-tuh-REE-uh
phrases.note: Ficar sem = to run out of (literally 'to end up without'). Nobody says the phone is 'dead' here.
Onde está...? = where is...? For more than one thing: onde estão as minhas sapatilhas?
If they know what you mean, shorten it to viste-o? — 'did you see it?', with o ('it') joined on by a hyphen.
Emprestar = to lend. Portuguese asks 'will you lend me...?' (emprestas-me...?) rather than 'can I borrow'.

phrases.pt: Qual é a palavra-passe do wi-fi?
phrases.ph: kwal eh uh puh-LAH-vruh pahs doo wye-FYE
phrases.note: A palavra-passe = password in Portugal; Brazilians say senha. Qual é...? = what is...? when asking for a specific thing.

phrases.pt: O wi-fi não está a funcionar.
phrases.ph: oo wye-FYE nown sh-TAH uh foon-syoo-NAR
phrases.note: Funcionar = to work, for machines. When people work, it's trabalhar.
Lenta = slow — feminine to match a internet. Mesmo here means 'really'.

phrases.en: Can you turn off the time limit?
phrases.pt: Podes tirar o limite de tempo?
phrases.ph: PO-dsh tee-RAR oo LEE-mee-tuh duh TAYN-poo
phrases.note: Tirar = to take off or remove. The same verb works for clothes: tira os sapatos = take your shoes off.
Dás-me...? = will you give me...? The me goes after the verb with a hyphen.
Só mais = just ... more. Só mais um = just one more — a line kids use a lot.
Bloqueaste = you blocked. The o ('it') comes before the verb because the question starts with porque é que.
Disto = de + isto ('of this'). Precisar always takes de, so 'I need this' becomes preciso disto.

phrases.pt: Estou a falar com as minhas amigas.
phrases.ph: sh-TOH uh fuh-LAR kohn uhzh MEE-nyuhz uh-MEE-guhsh
phrases.note: As minhas amigas means girl friends. For boys or a mixed group, say os meus amigos.
Estar quase a + verb = to be nearly doing something: estou quase a chegar = I'm nearly there.

phrases.en: Wait, I'm just replying to someone.
phrases.pt: Espera, estou só a responder a uma pessoa.
phrases.ph: sh-PEH-ruh, sh-TOH so uh rruhsh-pohn-DER uh OO-muh puh-SOH-uh
phrases.note: Uma pessoa = a person, used here for 'someone'. It's always feminine, even when the person is a boy.
Quase sem = almost without. Portuguese says 'I'm' out of battery, as if you were the phone.
O teu = your, for family and friends. To an adult you don't know well, you'd say o seu telemóvel.

phrases.pt: Podes partilhar os teus dados comigo?
phrases.ph: PO-dsh par-tee-LYAR oosh tewzh DAH-doosh koo-MEE-goo
phrases.note: Partilhar dados = to share mobile data — the everyday way to ask for a hotspot. Comigo = with me.
Os dados = mobile data, but the word also means 'dice'. Fiquei sem = I've run out of.
Rachado = cracked. O ecrã is 'screen' in Portugal; Brazilians say tela.
Descarregar = to download in Portugal (Brazil says baixar). It also means to unload, like a lorry.
Recebeste = did you get (from receber, to receive). A mensagem is feminine, so it's a minha.
Mando-te = I'll send you, with te ('you') hooked on after the verb. O link is borrowed straight from English.
Reiniciar = re + iniciar ('to start'), so 'restart'. Iniciar sessão is how you 'log in'.
Leias comes from ler (to read) — it's the form Portuguese uses for 'don't' orders: não leias!

phrases.en: Can you top up my phone?
phrases.note: Carregar also means 'to top up' with credit. The me ('for me') is attached to carregar with a hyphen.

phrases.pt: Para de chatear o teu irmão.
phrases.ph: PAH-ruh duh shuh-tee-AR oo tew eer-MOWN
phrases.note: Chatear = to annoy — hugely common in Portugal. Kids fire back with não me chateies! (stop bugging me!).

phrases.pt: Deixa o teu irmão em paz.
phrases.ph: DAY-shuh oo tew eer-MOWN ayn pash
phrases.note: Deixar em paz = to leave alone (literally 'leave in peace'). Deixa-me em paz! = leave me alone!
Discutir is a false friend: it means 'to argue', not 'to discuss'. Parem is 'stop' to more than one person.
Vocês os dois = the two of you. Vocês is the normal 'you' for several people in Portugal.
Aconteceu = happened, from acontecer. O que é que...? is the everyday way to ask 'what...?'.
Fizeste = you did, fiz = I did, fez = he or she did — all from fazer.

phrases.pt: O que é que ele fez?
phrases.note: Fez = he did. Swap ele for ela and it's 'what did she do?' — the verb stays the same.
Deitar as culpas a alguém = to blame someone (literally 'throw the blame'). Lhe = 'on him', placed before the verb after não.
Devolver = to give back or return. You'll also hear devolve-lho — 'give it back to him' (lho = lhe + o).
Dele = his, from de + ele ('of him'). Portuguese prefers it to seu because it's clearer.
Dela = hers, from de + ela ('of her'). One letter changes: dele is his, dela is hers.
Pedir = to ask for something (or for permission); perguntar = to ask a question. Tirar = to take.
Simpática is for a girl — a boy is simpático. It's a false friend: it means 'nice', not 'sympathetic'.
Provocar = to wind up or tease, not just 'provoke'. The o in the middle means 'him'.
Here ligar means 'to pay attention to', so não lhe ligues = don't pay him any attention. Lhe = him.
Deixa lá = let it go. Lá (literally 'there') softens it — you'll hear deixa lá everywhere in Portugal.
Chega! = enough! It comes from chegar, which means both 'to arrive' and 'to be enough'. Já chega! is even firmer.

phrases.en: I don't care who started it.
phrases.note: Quero lá saber = I couldn't care less (literally 'I want to know there'). Blunt — fine at home, rude to others.
Resolvam is the command for two or more people (vocês). Talking to just one kid, you'd say Resolve isso.
Pedir desculpa means 'to apologise' — literally 'ask for forgiveness'. Pede is the tu command.
Dá-lhe = 'give him': lhe ('to him') goes after the verb with a hyphen. Um pouco de = 'a bit of'.

phrases.en: Go away for five minutes and calm down.
phrases.pt: Sai daqui cinco minutos e acalma-te.
phrases.note: Acalma-te means 'calm yourself down' — the te ('yourself') sits after the verb with a hyphen. Sai daqui = 'get out of here'.
Parar de + verb = 'stop doing something'. Swap the verb: Para de chorar = stop crying.

phrases.en: Don't talk to him like that.
phrases.note: Fala! means 'talk!', but after não it changes to fales. Portuguese says 'talk with him' (falar com), not 'to him'.
À vez means 'in turns, one at a time'. Façam is the command for several people, from fazer (to do).
In Portugal 'to share' is partilhar; Brazilians say compartilhar. Partilhem is the command to two or more of you.
Queixinhas are 'little complaints', so fazer queixinhas is telling tales. A kid who always does it gets called um queixinhas.

phrases.en: You're both as bad as each other.
phrases.pt: São os dois farinha do mesmo saco.
phrases.ph: sown oozh doysh fuh-REE-nyuh doo MEZH-moo SAH-koo
phrases.note: Farinha do mesmo saco means 'flour from the same bag': two people who are just as bad as each other.
Com jeitinho means 'nicely, gently'. Jeito is a knack or way of doing things, and -inho makes it softer.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, you two.
phrases.pt: Vocês os dois, façam menos barulho.
phrases.note: Barulho = 'noise', so fazer menos barulho is 'make less noise'. Vocês os dois = 'you two'.

phrases.en: That's not how we talk to each other.
phrases.pt: Não é assim que falamos uns com os outros.
phrases.ph: nown eh uh-SEEM kuh fuh-LUH-moosh oonsh kohn oo-ZOH-troosh
phrases.note: Uns com os outros = 'with each other' (literally 'some with the others'). Não é assim que... = 'That's not how...'.
Foi ele que... = 'It was him who...' — the go-to pattern for blaming someone. Try Foi ela que partiu!
O quarto is your bedroom. No = em ('in') + o ('the') squashed together.
Diz-lhe para + verb = 'Tell him to...'. In Portugal the tu command is diz; the lhe ('him') follows with a hyphen.
Sair de = 'to get out of'. Do is de + o joined up, so do meu quarto = 'of my room'.
Imitar is copying what someone says or does; copiar is more for copying homework. Para de me imitar = 'stop copying me'.
Isso ('that') counts as masculine, so it's meu. For a named thing it matches: a bola é minha, o lápis é meu.
Justo = 'fair'. Don't mix it up with 'just' meaning 'only', which is só.

phrases.pt: Ele leva sempre a dele avante.
phrases.ph: AY-luh LEH-vuh SAYN-pruh uh DAY-luh uh-VAHNT
phrases.note: Levar a sua avante is an idiom for 'getting your own way'. In Portugal sempre usually comes after the verb: leva sempre.
Chato means 'annoying' or 'boring' (and literally 'flat'). For a girl it's chata.
És is 'you are' for one person you know well. Brazilians would say você é, but Portuguese families use és.
Word by word: deixa-me = 'leave me', em paz = 'in peace'. The me comes after the verb with a hyphen.
Está a chatear-me = 'is annoying me right now'. Estar a + verb is how Portugal says something is happening now.
Bater = 'to hit'. In Portugal it's bateu-me, with me after the verb; Brazilians say me bateu.
Estava = 'I was', from estar, used for where someone was. Primeiro = 'first'.
Devolver = 'to give back, return' — nothing to do with evolving! Devolve-me = 'give me back'.
Para com isso = 'stop that', literally 'stop with that'. Say it firmly and everyone gets it.
Ir-se embora = 'to go away'. Blunt — fine with your brother, rude to anyone else.

phrases.pt: Ele está a olhar para mim!
phrases.ph: AY-luh sh-TAH uh oh-LYAR PUH-ruh meen
phrases.note: Olhar needs para: olhar para alguém = 'look at someone'. After para, 'me' becomes mim.
Mexer em means 'to touch, mess about with'. Nas = em + as, so nas minhas coisas = 'in/on my things'.
Mentir = 'to lie' (tell fibs). Someone who lies is um mentiroso (or uma mentirosa for a girl).
Cala-te is rude-ish — OK between siblings, never to adults. Cala a boca ('shut your mouth') is even ruder.
Vez means 'turn' here, but also 'time', as in outra vez (again). Ask É a tua vez? for 'Is it your turn?'
Tirou-me = 'took from me', so Portuguese says 'the charger', not 'my charger'. O carregador = the charger.
In Portugal it's bebé; Brazilians write bebê. Mesmo here means 'really, such a'.
After não, the lhe ('him') jumps in front of the verb: não lhe toquei. Toquei = 'I touched'.
Portuguese usually puts o or a before names of people and pets: o Monty, a Sofia.
Cão is 'dog' in Portugal — Brazilians say cachorro, which in Portugal means a puppy.
Where English says 'have you seen', Portuguese uses the simple past: viste = 'did you see'.
Podes ...? = 'Can you ...?' — the easiest way to ask for help. Deixar sair = 'let out'.
Deixar + verb = 'let (someone) do something'. Deixa o cão entrar = 'let the dog come in'.
Entrar (go in) and sair (go out) are opposites — swap one word to flip the meaning.

phrases.en: Can you take Monty for a walk?
phrases.note: Passear o cão = 'walk the dog'. Passear on its own means going for a walk or a wander.

phrases.en: Has Monty been for a walk?
phrases.note: Já means 'already' or 'yet' — the key word in 'has it happened?' questions. Foi passear = 'went for a walk'.
Dar de comer = 'to feed', literally 'give to eat'. Deram = 'they gave', meaning anyone at all.

phrases.pt: Podes dar de comer ao cão?
phrases.ph: PO-dush dar duh koo-MER ow kown
phrases.note: Ao is a ('to') + o ('the'): dar de comer ao cão = 'give food to the dog'.
Dá-lhe = 'give him'. Dá has an accent, and lhe ('to him') follows with a hyphen.

phrases.pt: A tigela da água dele está vazia.
phrases.ph: uh tee-ZHEH-luh duh AH-gwuh DAY-luh sh-TAH vuh-ZEE-uh
phrases.note: Dele means 'his' and comes after the noun. Vazia ends in -a to match a tigela (the bowl).
A trela is the lead in Portugal. Don't confuse it with a coleira, which is the collar.
Põe is the tu command of pôr (to put). Põe-lhe = 'put on him', so no word for 'his' is needed.
Here o means 'him'. After não it moves before the verb, and deixa changes to deixes.
O portão is a gate — a big porta (door). The -ão ending often means a bigger version of something.
Chamar is calling someone over. Calling on the phone is ligar: Liga à avó = call Grandma.
Tirar = 'to take off, remove'. Tira-o = 'take him', with o ('him') after the verb.

phrases.pt: O que é que ele tem?
phrases.note: O que é que...? is a very Portuguese way to start a question — literally 'what is it that...?'
With tirar, lhe means 'from him': Tira-lhe isso = 'take that from him'.
Comida = 'food' (and also 'a meal'). Lhe can sit before dar here because de comes first.
Dá! ('give!') becomes não dês after não — keep the accent. Lhe jumps in front of the verb.

phrases.pt: O Monty precisa de fazer xixi.
phrases.ph: oo MON-tee pruh-SEE-zuh duh fuh-ZER shee-SHEE
phrases.note: In Portugal precisar needs de before the next word: precisa de fazer. Fazer xixi = 'do a wee'.
Apanhar = 'to pick up' (also 'to catch'). Poo is cocó in Portugal; Brazilians write cocô.

phrases.pt: Leva uns saquinhos para o cocó.
phrases.note: Saquinhos = 'little bags', from saco. Adding -inho makes things small: cão → cãozinho.

phrases.pt: Porque é que ele está a ladrar?
phrases.ph: POOR-kee eh kee-AY-luh sh-TAH uh luh-DRAR
phrases.note: In Portugal dogs ladrar (bark); Brazilians say latir. Porque é que...? = 'Why...?'

phrases.pt: Ele tem as patas cheias de lama.
phrases.ph: AY-luh tayn uhsh PAH-tuhsh SHAY-yuhzh duh LUH-muh
phrases.note: Word by word: tem = 'has', patas = 'paws', cheias de lama = 'full of mud'.
With body parts Portuguese says 'dry to him the paws' (seca-lhe as patas) rather than 'his paws'.

phrases.en: Don't let him on the bed.
phrases.pt: Não o deixes subir para a cama.
phrases.ph: nown oo DAY-shush soo-BEER PUH-ruh uh KUH-muh
phrases.note: Subir = 'to climb up, go up'. Subir para a cama = 'get up onto the bed'.
Watch out: a pill is um comprimido; um tablet is the computer. Tomar = 'to take' medicine.
Dogs just hear Senta! A person would be told Senta-te! ('sit yourself down').
Portuguese families often call dog treats biscoitos ('biscuits'). Um prémio ('a reward') works too.
Vomitou = 'threw up'. Careful: estar doente means 'to be ill', not 'to be sick' in the vomiting sense.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.pt: O Monty pode dormir no meu quarto?
phrases.ph: oo MON-tee pod door-MEER noo mayoo KWAR-too
phrases.note: Pode = 'can he/she', posso = 'can I'. Just raise your voice at the end to make it a question.
Uma meia is a sock (and meias can also be tights). Roubou-me = 'stole from me'.

phrases.en: Do I have to walk him?
phrases.pt: Tenho de o levar a passear?
phrases.note: Tenho de = 'I have to' — Portugal uses de, while Brazilians usually say tenho que.
Giro is Portugal's word for 'cute' or 'nice-looking' — Brazilians don't use it. For a girl dog: tão gira.
Cheirar mal = 'to smell bad'. The opposite is cheira bem — 'smells nice'.
Um banho is a bath or shower. Tomar banho = 'to have a bath/shower'.
Menino = 'little boy'. People talk to dogs like small kids, so menino bonito is the usual 'good boy'.

phrases.pt: Alguém já lhe deu de comer?
phrases.ph: al-GAYN zhah lyuh dayoo duh koo-MER
phrases.note: Alguém = 'someone/anyone'; its opposite is ninguém ('nobody').

phrases.pt: Ele está a ladrar outra vez.
phrases.ph: AY-luh sh-TAH uh luh-DRAR OH-truh vaysh
phrases.note: Outra vez = 'again', literally 'another time'. De novo means the same thing.
Descer = 'to get down, go down', and subir is its opposite. Desce also works for 'come downstairs!'.
A one-word order from sentar. A teacher telling the whole class to sit says Sentem-se!
Anda cá is Portugal's 'come here' (literally 'walk here'); Brazilians say vem cá.
Largar = 'to let go, drop'. False friend: it has nothing to do with 'large' (which is grande).
Lindo menino = 'lovely boy', the classic praise for a dog. A girl dog is a linda menina.
Lamber = 'to lick'. The me ('me') joins the end of the verb with a hyphen: lamber-me.

phrases.pt: Ele está outra vez na minha cama.
phrases.ph: AY-luh sh-TAH OH-truh vayzh nuh MEE-nyuh KUH-muh
phrases.note: Na = em + a, so na minha cama = 'on my bed'. Portuguese often tucks outra vez into the middle of a sentence.

phrases.en: Can I give him a treat?
phrases.note: Posso ...? = 'Can I ...?' — use it to ask permission for anything. Dar-lhe = 'give him'.

phrases.en: It's not my turn to walk him.
phrases.pt: Não é a minha vez de o levar a passear.
phrases.ph: nown eh uh MEE-nyuh vayzh dyoo luh-VAR uh puh-see-AR
phrases.note: A minha vez de + verb = 'my turn to...'. Levar a passear = 'take for a walk'.
Deixar means both 'to leave' and 'to let', so Deixa isso = 'leave that alone'.
Aonde = 'to where', used with verbs of going. Vais is 'you go' for one person.
In chatty Portuguese the question word can go at the end: Vais com quem? = 'You're going with who?'
Quem = 'who'. Adding é que makes it sound natural in speech — very common in Portugal.

phrases.en: What are you going to do?
phrases.note: Vais fazer = 'are going to do'. Ir + verb talks about the future, just like 'going to' in English.
A que horas...? = 'At what time...?' Answer with às: às seis = at six.

phrases.en: What time will you be back?
phrases.note: Voltas = 'you come back'. Portuguese often uses the present tense for plans later today.

phrases.pt: Como é que vais para lá?
phrases.ph: KOH-moo eh kuh vysh PUH-ruh lah
phrases.note: Lá = 'there' (over there). Answers: de autocarro (by bus), de comboio (by train), a pé (on foot).
Boleia is a lift in a car in Portugal; Brazilians say carona.

phrases.en: Do you want me to take you?
phrases.note: Queres que eu... = 'Do you want me to...?' The verb after que changes: levo becomes leve.
Ir buscar = 'to go and get, pick up'. Vou buscar-te = 'I'll come and get you'.

phrases.en: Message me when you get there.
phrases.note: Manda-me mensagem = 'send me a message'. After quando for the future, chegas becomes chegares.

phrases.en: Let me know if your plans change.
phrases.note: False friend: avisar means 'to let know, warn', not 'advise' (that's aconselhar).
In Portugal a phone is o telemóvel; Brazilians say celular. Ligado = 'switched on'.

phrases.en: Make sure your phone has some charge.
phrases.pt: Vê se o telemóvel tem bateria.
phrases.note: Vê se... = 'make sure / check that...' (literally 'see if'). Ter bateria = 'to have charge'.
Tens = 'have you got'. Suficiente usually comes after the noun: dinheiro suficiente.
Contigo = 'with you' (one word, not com ti). Comigo = 'with me'.
Levar = 'take (with you)', trazer = 'bring'. Leva for things going out; Traz for things coming here.
Lá fora = 'outside' (out there). Weather uses estar: está frio, está calor.
Está a chover = 'it's raining right now'. In Portugal it's estar a + verb; Brazilians say está chovendo.
Venhas comes from vir ('to come'); after não, vem changes to venhas. Literally 'don't come very late'.
Tem cuidado is literally 'have care'. To a group: Tenham cuidado.
Diverte-te = 'enjoy yourself'. The te ('yourself') follows the verb with a hyphen.
Até logo = 'see you later'. Até já is for very soon; até amanhã is 'see you tomorrow'.
Combinar = 'to arrange, agree to meet'. Combinaram is the vocês form, for you and your friends.
In Portugal you conduzir a car; Brazilians say dirigir. A driving licence is a carta de condução.

phrases.en: Will there be an adult there?
phrases.note: Vai estar = 'will be'. Algum adulto = 'any adult' in a question.
Juntas is for a group of girls; boys or a mixed group is juntos. Fiquem = 'stay' to several people.

phrases.en: Don't go off on your own.
phrases.pt: Não vás sozinha para lado nenhum.
phrases.ph: nown vahsh soo-ZEE-nyuh PUH-ruh LAH-doo nuh-NYOON
phrases.note: Sozinha is for a girl — a boy is sozinho. Para lado nenhum = 'anywhere' after não.
Portuguese often says 'the keys' (as chaves) where English says 'your keys' — it's obvious whose.
Atender = 'to answer' the phone, and ligar = 'to call'. Responder is for answering a question.
Direta is for a girl — a boy is direto. Para casa = 'home' when you're heading there.

phrases.en: I'll pick you up at ten.
phrases.note: Às dez = 'at ten'. Às is a + as (horas): às três, às oito — but à uma for one o'clock.

phrases.en: Say hi to them from me.
phrases.note: Beijinhos ('little kisses') is how Portuguese families send hi or love. Lhes = 'to them'.
Sair = 'to go out' or 'to leave'. Posso sair com os meus amigos? adds 'with my friends'.
Podemos = 'we can'. Podemos + verb works for asking permission for the whole group.
Levar-me = 'take me', with me hooked on after a hyphen. Shorter and just as common: Levas-me?

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift?
phrases.note: Boleia is the Portuguese word for a lift in a car; Brazilians say carona. Dar boleia = to give a lift.
Ir buscar means 'go and fetch', which is how Portuguese says 'pick up' a person. The me ('me') is stuck on the end with a hyphen.
Levar = to take someone somewhere, and nos = 'us'. Lá means 'there', far from both of you.

phrases.en: Can you pick us up later?
phrases.note: Mais logo is a very Portuguese way to say 'later today'. You'll hear it all the time in Portugal but rarely in Brazil.

phrases.pt: A minha amiga pode vir cá a casa?
phrases.ph: uh MEE-nyuh uh-MEE-guh pod veer kah uh KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Cá a casa means 'here to our house'. Amiga is a girl friend; for a boy say o meu amigo.

phrases.en: Can I have a friend over?
phrases.pt: Posso trazer uma amiga cá a casa?
phrases.ph: PO-soo truh-ZER OO-muh uh-MEE-guh kah uh KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Posso ...? = Can I ...? It's the easiest way to ask permission. Trazer = to bring; uma amiga becomes um amigo for a boy.
Cá means 'here, where I am', so vir cá is 'come round'. Its opposite is lá, 'over there'.
Ficar = to stay. Jantar is both 'dinner' and 'to have dinner', so ficar para jantar is 'stay for dinner'.

phrases.pt: Ela pode ficar cá a dormir esta noite?
phrases.ph: EH-luh pod fee-KAR kah uh door-MEER ESH-tuh noyt
