phrases.note: Ficar a dormir, literally 'stay sleeping', is how Portuguese says 'stay over'. Esta noite = tonight.

phrases.en: Can I stay at her house?
phrases.note: Dela means 'her' or 'hers' (de + ela) and goes after the thing: casa dela = her house. For a boy, casa dele.
Lá ('there') shows you mean at the friend's house. Ficar a dormir is the everyday way to say 'sleep over'.

phrases.en: What time do I have to be home?
phrases.pt: A que horas tenho de estar em casa?
phrases.ph: uh kee-O-ruhsh TUH-nyoo duh sh-TAH-rayn KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Tenho de = I have to. In Portugal people say ter de; Brazilians usually say ter que.

phrases.en: Do I have to come home that early?
phrases.pt: Tenho mesmo de voltar tão cedo?
phrases.ph: TUH-nyoo MEZH-moo duh vol-TAR town SAY-doo
phrases.note: Mesmo adds 'really' to a complaint: Tenho mesmo de...? = Do I really have to...? Cedo = early; tão cedo = that early.

phrases.pt: Os outros todos ficam até mais tarde.
phrases.ph: oo-ZOH-troosh TOH-doosh FEE-kown uh-TEH mysh tard
phrases.note: Os outros todos means 'all the others'. Portuguese often uses the present tense, ficam ('they stay'), for plans tonight.
Mando-te = I'll send you. In Portugal the te ('you') goes after the verb with a hyphen; Brazilians put it before.
Avisar means 'to let someone know' or 'to warn', not 'to advise'. Depois = afterwards, later.
A caminho = on the way (caminho is 'path' or 'way'). Handy for texting: Estou a caminho!
Estamos a sair uses estar a + verb for something happening right now. Brazilians would say estamos saindo.
Quase = almost. Estar quase a + verb means 'to be about to': quase a chegar = nearly arriving.
Word by word: já (already) cá (here) estou (I am). Portuguese puts cá before estou in this short phrase.
Cá fora = out here, where I am. If someone else is outside, it's lá fora ('out there').
Estás is the tu form of estar, used for where someone is right now. In Portugal, never use você with family.
Demorar = to take (time) or to be long. Quanto tempo = how much time. Try Não demores! = Don't be long!
Despachar-se is the Portuguese go-to for 'hurry up'. The te ('yourself') sits after the verb with a hyphen.

phrases.en: Can I go to the cinema?
phrases.note: Ao is a + o ('to the') squashed together. With a feminine place it's à: ir à praia (go to the beach).

phrases.en: I'm going to my friend's house.
phrases.pt: Vou a casa da minha amiga.
phrases.ph: voh uh KAH-zuh duh MEE-nyuh uh-MEE-guh
phrases.note: A casa de = to someone's house, with no 'the' before casa. For a boy friend: a casa do meu amigo.
Combinámos = we arranged. In Portugal the past 'we' form has an accent (combinámos) to tell it apart from 'we arrange'.

phrases.en: Can I go to a party on Saturday?
phrases.pt: Posso ir a uma festa no sábado?
phrases.ph: PO-soo eer uh OO-muh FESH-tuh noo SAH-buh-doo
phrases.note: No sábado = on Saturday (no is em + o). Days of the week start with a small letter in Portuguese.
Aniversário means 'birthday' as well as 'anniversary'. Parabéns! is what you say to the birthday girl.

phrases.pt: Hoje à noite fico em casa.
phrases.note: Hoje à noite = tonight (literally 'today at night'). Ficar em casa = to stay in.

phrases.en: Her mum will bring me back.
phrases.pt: A mãe dela traz-me a casa.
phrases.ph: uh mayn DEH-luh TRAHZH-muh uh KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Trazer = to bring (towards here) and levar = to take (away). Traz-me: the me goes after the verb with a hyphen.

phrases.en: Can I stay a bit longer?
phrases.note: Bocadinho means 'a little bit' and is used everywhere in Portugal. Mais um bocadinho = a bit more.
In Portugal até às dez means 'by ten' (at ten at the latest). Às dez alone = at ten.

phrases.en: Wait for me in the car.
phrases.note: Portuguese needs por after esperar for 'wait for': espera por mim. Mim is the 'me' used after little words like por.
Anda cá is how Portuguese parents say 'come here' (literally 'walk here'). Brazilians say vem cá.
Ir-se embora = to go away. Vai-te embora is firm; just Vai embora sounds a bit more Brazilian.
To tell one person to do something, use the tu present without the s: esperas (you wait) becomes Espera!
Aí means 'there, near you', different from lá, 'over there, away from us both'.
Ouvir means both 'to hear' and 'to listen'. Ouve is the command for one person; to a group, Ouçam.
Olha is also used to get attention, like 'Look, ...' at the start of a sentence: Olha, não tenho tempo.
Para is the command from parar (to stop). It's spelt the same as para ('for') — the old accent pára was dropped.
Nem penses literally means 'don't even think (about it)' — the short, firm way a Portuguese parent says 'Don't.'
After não, commands change form: faz (do) becomes não faças (don't do). Isso = that (near you).
Deixa isso = leave that alone. Watch out: Deixa estar means 'never mind, don't bother'.
Pousar = to put down or set down (it's also what birds do when they land). Pousa isso = put that down.
Dá-me = give me, from dar. You'll also hear the shorter Dá cá! ('Give it here!').
Traz is the command form of trazer (to bring) — it's irregular, so learn it by heart. Cá = here.
Toma, from tomar, is what you say as you hand something over. On its own it means 'here you go'.
Segurar = to hold. Isto means 'this, near me' — compare isso, 'that, near you'.
Ajuda-me: the me ('me') comes after the verb with a hyphen. As a polite question: Ajudas-me?
Cuidado means 'care', and shouted on its own it's the quick warning 'Watch out!'
Tem cuidado is literally 'have care'. Tem here is the command form of ter (to have).
Despacha-te is what every Portuguese kid hears in the morning. The te ('yourself') goes after the verb.
Devagar = slowly, so mais devagar = more slowly. Say it twice for a relaxed 'take it easy': devagar, devagar.
Acalmar-se = to calm (yourself) down. Try saying it calmly, or it tends to have the opposite effect!
A sério? is the Portugal way to say 'Seriously?' Brazilians tend to say Sério? without the a.

phrases.pt: O que é que estás a fazer?
phrases.note: Estás a fazer = you're doing (right now), using estar a + verb. Brazilians say está fazendo instead.
Fizeste literally means 'you did'. Portuguese uses this simple past where English says 'have done'.
On its own or at the end of a question, 'why' is porquê, one word with an accent. At the start: Porque é que...?
Como = how. Said with a puzzled face, Como? also means 'Pardon?' when you didn't hear something.
Onde = where. For 'where to?' add a: Aonde? — e.g. Aonde vais? (Where are you going?)
Quando = when. Useful follow-up: Até quando? = Until when?
Quem = who, and disse = said (from dizer). Quem disse? on its own also works.

phrases.pt: O que queres dizer com isso?
phrases.note: Querer dizer, literally 'to want to say', means 'to mean'. Com isso = by that.
After já ('already') the te ('you') jumps in front of the verb: já te disse, not já disse-te.
Pedir = to ask for something; perguntar = to ask a question. Here the parent asked you to do something, so pedi.
Portuguese flips the order: agora não, literally 'now not'. Same with Hoje não (not today).
Daqui a + time = in (that long from now): daqui a um minuto, daqui a uma hora. Don't use em here.
Depois means 'later' or 'afterwards'. Depois vemos = we'll see later; depois de = after.
Talvez = maybe. Careful: the Spanish-looking pode ser means 'that works' or 'OK' in Portugal, not 'maybe'.
Logo se vê is a classic Portuguese parent answer — literally 'soon it will be seen'. It usually means 'probably not'.
Nem pensar, literally 'not even to think', is a flat no. No argument is expected after it.
Pode ser literally means 'it can be', but in Portugal it's a way to agree: 'fine, that works'.
Vá lá is 'go on' — used to give in, or to urge someone on. Está bem = okay (often shortened to 'tá bem).
Chegar means 'to arrive', but chega also means 'that's enough'. Já chega! = that's quite enough now.
Olhar needs para for 'look at': olha para mim = look at me. Mim is the 'me' used after para.
Cala-te is 'shut up' — blunt, fine from a parent, rude to anyone else. Softer: Fala baixo.
Word by word: fala (speak) mais (more) baixo (low). Baixo means 'low' or 'short', never 'bass'.
Responder = to answer (think 'respond'). The me goes after the verb with a hyphen in a command.

phrases.en: Don't talk to me like that.
phrases.note: With não, me moves before the verb and fala becomes fales. Assim = like that.
Brincar means 'to play' (like little kids do) and also 'to joke'. Estás a brincar? = Are you kidding?
Claro means 'clear' as well as 'of course'. Make it stronger with Claro que sim! (Of course, yes!)
At the end of a question or on its own, 'what' is o quê, with an accent. Blunter than Diga? or Como?
Já vou! literally means 'I'm already going!' — the classic shout back when your mum or dad calls you.
Lá here isn't 'there' — it just softens and stretches the word, like 'hang on a sec'.
Não also means 'not'. For a really stubborn no, say Não e não! (No means no!)
Porquê eu? — porquê needs its accent when there's no verb after it. Add sempre for extra drama: Porquê sempre eu?
Já vai! (literally 'it's already going') is what Portuguese kids shout when they mean 'just a sec, I'm on it'.
Pronto usually means 'ready', but in Portugal it's also a grumpy 'fine, OK then'. A boy says it the same way here.
Parar com = to stop doing something. Para com isso! is 'stop that!' — handy for annoying brothers.
Sai da frente! means 'get out of the way' (literally 'leave the front'). Blunt — fine with your brother.
Devolver = to give back or return (not 'devolve'). Devolve-me isso = give that back to me.
Chiu! is the Portuguese 'Shh!' Put a finger on your lips as you say it.
Ocupada is for a girl — a boy says ocupado. Estar is used because being busy doesn't last.
Adding lá to a command makes it pushier, like 'come on, hurry up!' Despacha-te = hurry (yourself) up.
Olha só! = 'just look!' The só ('only') adds excitement, as if you've spotted something amazing.
Desaparece! literally means 'disappear!' Rude-ish — keep it for brothers, not for grown-ups.
Tanto faz, literally 'it makes as much', means 'I don't care either way'. Can sound a bit rude to parents.
Portuguese puts não after the person here: Eu não! = not me. Likewise Ele não! = not him.
Fui is 'I was' from ser — and also 'I went' from ir. Não fui eu! = it wasn't me.
To one person it's Espera por mim!; to a group of friends it becomes Esperem por mim!
Em paz means 'in peace', so this is 'leave me in peace'. Deixa-me = leave me, with me after the verb.
Como estás? uses tu, right for family and friends. You'd say Como está? to a teacher.
Então ('so' or 'then') is a favourite Portuguese conversation starter. Tudo bem? = all good?
Sabes uma coisa? literally means 'Do you know a thing?' — a way to build up to some news.
Correr means 'to run', but correr bem/mal means 'to go well/badly'. Correu bem! = It went well!
Contar means both 'to tell' and 'to count'. Conta-me tudo = tell me everything.
Ai sim? is a surprised 'Oh really?' Ai is a little sound Portuguese people use for surprise, worry or pain.
Que + adjective = How ...! So que bom = how good. A kid might say Que fixe! (How cool!)
Ai is the Portuguese 'oh' or 'ow' — you'll hear Ai! when someone stubs a toe too.
Literally 'What is it that you have?' Portuguese uses ter (to have) to ask what's wrong with someone.
Era = was, from ser. Handy after the doorbell or a phone call: Quem era?
Achar = to think (have an opinion). In Portugal 'to find' something is encontrar.
Acreditar = to believe. Não acredito! literally 'I don't believe' — no 'it' needed in Portuguese.
Ir para = to go to (and stay a while). O trabalho = work, the place and the job.
Volto (I come back) is present tense but means 'I'll be back'. Às seis = at six o'clock.
Adoro-te is how Portuguese families usually say 'I love you'; amo-te sounds stronger, more romantic.

phrases.pt: Então, o que andas a fazer?
phrases.note: Andar a + verb means 'to be busy doing something' lately or right now. Andas a fazer = you're up to.
Portuguese keeps 'the' before 'your': o teu dia, literally 'the your day'. Foi = was.
Estás bem? — just 'are you well?'. Answer Estou bem (I'm fine) or Mais ou menos (so-so).
Cansado is how a dad says it — a mum says cansada. Tão = so.
Que + noun = What a ...! No word for 'a' needed: Que dia! Que seca! (What a drag!)
Cheguei! literally means 'I've arrived!' — what Portuguese people call out when they walk in the door.
After não, te goes before the verb, and preocupa changes to preocupes for a 'don't' command.
Tudo = everything, and bem = well. Tudo bem? on its own is also a friendly 'hi, how's it going?'
Portuguese says 'I have a lot of pride in you': ter orgulho em. Ti is the 'you' used after em.

phrases.en: Did you have a good time?
phrases.note: Divertiste-te means 'did you enjoy yourself?'. The te ('yourself') goes after the verb with a hyphen.
Pai is what Portuguese kids of your age call their dad. Papá sounds more like a little child.
Mãe is 'Mum'. Don't forget the squiggle (a tilde) on the ã. Mamã is what small children say.
O quê? is the everyday 'What?'. If you want to sound more polite with a parent, try Desculpa? ('Sorry?').
Estás a fazer = 'you are doing' right now. In Portugal it's estar a + verb; Brazilians say estás fazendo.
Onde = where. For where someone is, use estar (estás), not ser.
Aonde means 'to where' and goes with movement verbs like ir. Vais is 'you go' from ir.
When talking about Mum, Portuguese adds 'the': a mãe. Without the a it sounds odd.
O pai is literally 'the dad'. That's how Portuguese families talk about Dad.
In Portugal people put o or a before names: o Monty, a Sofia. It sounds friendly, not strange.
Literally 'What hours are they?'. The answer is plural too: São cinco horas (it's five o'clock).
Hoje means 'today', and Portuguese people normally add it here. Answer: Hoje é sexta-feira.
A que horas...? = 'At what time...?'. Saímos is 'we leave'. Portuguese often uses the present for plans.
Vamos + verb = 'we're going to...'. Handy pattern: Vamos comer? (Are we going to eat?)
Algum lado means 'somewhere' or 'anywhere'. Lado is 'side', so it's literally 'to some side'.
Já here means 'now' or 'yet'. Podemos = 'we can'. Já podemos...? is a great way to hurry parents up.
Pronto is for asking Dad. To Mum, say Estás pronta? Careful: pronto on its own can also mean 'right then'.

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.note: Demorar means 'to take a long time'. Vais demorar muito? (Will you be long?) is a shorter way to ask.
Anda comes from andar (to walk), but in Portugal it's used to mean 'come on' or 'come here'.
Olhar needs para: olha para isto = look at this. Olha! on its own is also like 'Hey, look!'
Vê comes from ver (to see/watch). Use it when you're about to show a trick or a video.
Ouve is the command form of ouvir (to hear). No word for 'to' needed: just ouve isto.
Adivinha is the command 'guess!' from adivinhar. Add something like Adivinha quem ligou! (Guess who called!)
Aconteceu = 'happened', from acontecer. Sabes...? = 'Do you know...?', a useful way to start any story.

phrases.pt: Nunca vais adivinhar o que aconteceu.
phrases.note: Nunca vais adivinhar = 'you're never going to guess'. Nunca (never) goes before the verb.
Piada means 'joke', so tem piada is literally 'it has a joke' – that's how you say something is funny.
Estranho = strange or weird. Que + describing word = 'How ...!' – Que giro! (How cute!)
Chatice is an annoying thing or a hassle. It comes from chato (annoying), a word you'll hear all the time.
Nojo means 'disgust'. Que nojo! is what any Portuguese kid shouts at a sock that smells.
Vergonha means both 'embarrassment' and 'shame'. Tenho vergonha = I'm embarrassed.
Justo means 'fair', not 'just'. Não before the verb makes it negative: não é = isn't.
Literally 'I don't want to know'. Quite blunt – fine at home, but it can sound rude to others.
Sei is 'I know' from saber. Put não in front and you've got the answer to half of all questions.
Se calhar is the everyday Portuguese 'maybe' – you'll hear it more than talvez, which means the same.
The -mente ending is like English '-ly': provável (probable) becomes provavelmente (probably).
Pronto usually means 'ready', but on its own it's a very Portuguese 'fine' or 'OK then'.
Está bem is literally 'it is well'. People often squash it into tá bem when talking fast.
Tanto faz is like 'it makes no difference'. Said with a shrug it sounds as dismissive as 'whatever'.
In Portugal you say a sério? with the a. Brazilians just say sério?
Mesmo usually means 'same', but on its own as a question it means 'Really?'
Nem pensar is literally 'not even think (about it)'. Use it to refuse something firmly.
Obviamente is the full word; lots of kids just say Óbvio! for a snappier 'Obviously!'
Exatamente is spelt without a c in modern European Portuguese. Exato! is a shorter version.
Sei is 'I know' from saber. Adding eu (I) gives it extra punch. Já sei! means 'I already know!'
This para is the command form of parar (to stop). It's not the other para, which means 'for'.
Literally 'leave me in peace'. The me goes after deixa with a hyphen, as in most commands.
Embora means 'away'. Vai-te embora is blunt – fine with a brother, rude to anyone else.
Chata is for a girl or woman, chato for a boy or man. És is 'you are' from ser.
Tão means 'so'. To your brother or Dad it's És tão chato! Cheeky, so watch your tone.
Girls say obrigada and boys say obrigado – it depends on who is thanking, not who is thanked.
Não foi por mal is literally 'it wasn't for bad' – the Portuguese way to say you didn't mean it.
Adoro-te is how Portuguese families say 'love you'. Amo-te is stronger and mostly used for partners.
In Portugal aborrecida means 'bored' (in Brazil it means annoyed). A boy says aborrecido.
Fixe is the Portuguese word for 'cool' – you'll hear it everywhere in Portugal but not in Brazil.

phrases.pt: Não faz mal, não te preocupes.
phrases.ph: nown fahsh mahl, nown tuh pree-oo-KOO-push
phrases.note: Não faz mal = 'it doesn't matter', literally 'it does no harm'. A kind thing to say after a mistake.
Posso...? = 'Can I...?'. The te ('you') is stuck to the end of perguntar with a hyphen.
Brincar means 'to play' and also 'to joke'. Estou a brincar = I'm joking right now.
Literally 'I've already arrived!' – it's what Portuguese kids shout when they walk through the door.
Também = 'too' or 'also'. For 'me neither', say Eu também não.
Estás bem? is 'Are you well?'. Just answer Estou bem (I'm fine) or Mais ou menos (so-so).
Literally 'What is it that you have?'. Portuguese people love adding é que to questions.
Pareces = 'you seem'. In Portugal chateada means upset or annoyed; for a boy it's chateado.
Sentir-se = to feel. In a yes/no question the te still goes after the verb: sentes-te.
A plaster in Portugal is um penso rápido ('quick dressing'). Precisar always needs de after it.
Dói = 'it hurts'. After a question word like onde, the te moves in front of the verb.

phrases.en: Do you want to talk about it?
phrases.note: Queres...? = 'Do you want to...?'. Sobre isso = 'about that'. A useful pattern for lots of offers.
After não, the te goes before the verb: não te preocupes. Compare Preocupa-te! (Worry!)

phrases.en: Try not to stress about your exams.
phrases.pt: Tenta não te enervar com os exames.
phrases.ph: TAYN-tuh nown tuh ee-nur-VAR kohn oo-zee-ZUH-mush
phrases.note: Enervar-se means 'to get worked up' – it doesn't mean 'enervate'. Tenta não... = 'try not to...'.
Devias = 'you should', from dever. Handy pattern: Devias + any verb, e.g. Devias dormir.
Literally 'you've got a tired face'. Cansada is for a girl; to a boy it's cara de cansado.
Já ('yet/now') pulls the te in front of the verb. Melhor = better; pior = worse.
Rabugenta means 'grumpy' – rabugento for a boy. Estar (estás) is used because the mood is just for today.
Anima-te is literally 'liven yourself up'. The te goes after the verb, with a hyphen.
Não sejas = 'don't be', a special form of ser used after não. To a boy: tão dramático.
Tomar is used for taking medicine (and having a shower: tomar banho). Toma = take.

phrases.en: Do you need to see the doctor?
phrases.note: Literally 'do you need to go to the doctor?'. Ao is a + o squashed together: 'to the'.
Na = em + a ('in the'). Alguma coisa = 'something' – literally 'some thing'.

phrases.en: Go and lie down for a bit.
phrases.note: Um bocadinho ('a little bit') is very Portuguese. Deitar-se = to lie down, so it's deitar-te for you.
Ferver means 'to boil', so it's literally 'you're boiling!' – said when a kid has a high temperature.
Bebeste is 'you drank', the tu past form of beber. Já here means 'yet' or 'so far'.

phrases.en: It's not the end of the world.
phrases.pt: Não é o fim do mundo.
phrases.ph: nown eh oo feen doo MOON-doo
phrases.note: Almost word for word: fim = end, do = of the, mundo = world. Easy to remember!
Sinto is 'I feel'. Because of não, the me jumps in front: não me sinto, but Sinto-me bem.
Literally 'the head hurts me'. Swap the body part: Dói-me o pé (my foot hurts).
Barriga means 'tummy'. Portuguese uses a (the) where English says 'my' for body parts.
Garganta = throat. Tenho dores de... ('I have pains of...') is another way to say something hurts.

phrases.en: I think I've got a temperature.
phrases.note: Acho que... = 'I think...'. Febre is 'fever' – that's what Portuguese says for a temperature.
Preocupada is for a girl, preocupado for a boy. Notice com ('with') where English says 'about'.
Portuguese borrowed 'stress' from English: stressada (girl) or stressado (boy).
Abraço = hug. Portuguese people also sign off messages with Um abraço! ('A hug!')
Farta literally means 'full up' (from eating). A boy says Estou farto. Add de: Estou farta de chuva.
Estou is 'I am' from estar, used for how you feel right now. Bem = well.
Deixa-me = 'leave me'; em paz = 'in peace'. To several people at once, say Deixem-me em paz.
In Portugal perceber is the usual word for 'understand'; Brazilians prefer entender.
Enjoada means 'feeling sick' – also 'carsick'. A boy says enjoado.

phrases.pt: A cabeça está a dar cabo de mim.
phrases.ph: uh kuh-BAY-suh sh-TAH uh dar KAH-boo duh meen
phrases.note: Dar cabo de means 'to wreck' or 'finish off' – a very Portuguese phrase. Literally 'my head is finishing me off'.
O período is 'period' – careful, it's also the word for a school term!
Que stress! is a quick way to moan about stress. It uses the English word, with the same meaning.
Seca means 'drought', but Que seca! is Portuguese slang for 'How boring!'
Mau humor = bad mood. Watch out: mal-disposta doesn't mean grumpy in Portugal – it means feeling sick.
Só = 'only' or 'just'. Só quero... is a handy start: Só quero comer (I just want to eat).
Literally 'I'm dying of hunger!'. Estar a + verb shows it's happening now.
Apetecer means 'to feel like'. It's used all the time in Portugal: Apetece-me um gelado (I fancy an ice cream).

phrases.en: It's been the worst day ever.
phrases.pt: Foi o pior dia de sempre.
phrases.ph: foy oo pee-OR DEE-uh duh SAYN-pruh
phrases.note: De sempre means 'ever' here. O melhor dia de sempre = the best day ever.
De rastos means 'dragging yourself along the ground' – so tired you can barely move. Same for girls and boys.
Exagerar has only one g, unlike 'exaggerate'. Estou a exagerar = I'm exaggerating (right now).

phrases.en: I don't want to talk about it.
phrases.note: Disso is de + isso ('of that') joined up. Falar de = to talk about.

phrases.en: I think I'm getting a cold.
phrases.pt: Acho que estou a ficar constipada.
phrases.ph: AH-shoo kee sh-TOH uh fee-KAR kohnsh-tee-PAH-duh
phrases.note: False friend: constipada means 'has a cold', not constipated! A boy says constipado.
Literally 'I have pride in you'. Orgulho doesn't change, so Mum and Dad can both say it.
Desistir = to give up. After não, commands take a special form: não desistas.
Conseguir means 'to manage' or 'succeed'. Consegues? on its own = 'Can you manage?'
Sorte (luck) is a feminine word, so it's boa, not bom. Que sorte! = How lucky!
Ficou means 'it turned out'. Espetacular is spelt without a c in modern European Portuguese.
Ajudares has -es to show it's you who helped. Dad says obrigado; Mum would say obrigada.
Gostar de = to like, but gosto muito de ti is a warm family 'love you lots'. Ti = you after de.
Linda means 'beautiful'. To a boy say Estás lindo, or Estás muito giro (you look really nice).
Continua = 'carry on', assim = 'like this'. Easy to spot from English 'continue'.

phrases.en: It doesn't matter if you get it wrong.
phrases.pt: Não faz mal se te enganares.
phrases.ph: nown fahsh mahl suh tuh ayn-guh-NAH-rush
phrases.note: Enganar-se = to make a mistake. Se te enganares = 'if you get it wrong'; the te comes first after se.
Literally 'do the best that you can'. Puderes is a special 'if/when' form of poder (can).
Ter jeito para = to be good at something. Jeito means knack or skill – a very useful word.
Parabéns is for well done AND for birthdays. The accent on the é matters.
Querida means 'sweet' or 'kind' (and 'dear'). For a boy it's És tão querido.
Muito bem = 'very well'. Teachers say it too, so listen out for it in class.

phrases.en: I knew you could do it.
phrases.note: Sabia = 'I knew', conseguias = 'you could manage'. Both are past forms for things that went on over time.
Nota = mark. In Portuguese schools a 5 is top up to year 9; older students get marks out of 20.
Esforçar-se = to make an effort. Imenso means 'loads' – Portuguese people use it a lot.
In Portugal brutal means 'awesome', not violent. Espetacular! is a slightly less slangy option.

phrases.pt: Não faz mal, fica para a próxima.
phrases.ph: nown fahsh mahl, FEE-kuh pruh PRO-see-muh
phrases.note: Fica para a próxima = 'it'll be for next time' — a handy way to shrug off something that didn't go well.
Fiz is 'I did', from fazer (to do). No extra question word needed — just raise your voice at the end.
Consegui comes from conseguir, 'to manage'. One word says the whole 'I did it!'.
És is 'you are' when talking to one person as tu. A melhor is for Mum; to Dad say És o melhor!
Tive = 'I had', from ter. Portuguese says 'I had a good mark' rather than 'I got'.
Ter jeito para = 'to have a knack for'. Try it: Tens jeito para música? = Are you good at music?
Mãe is 'Mum' and pai is 'Dad'. A boy would say obrigado instead of obrigada.
Bem adds 'I really did' punch. Because bem comes before the verb, te ('you') moves in front of disse.
Orgulhosa is for a girl — a boy says orgulhoso. De mim = 'of me'.
Espetacular is a favourite Portuguese word for 'amazing'. Que espetáculo! means the same.
Muito bem ('very well') is the everyday 'well done'. Careful: pai is Dad, but pais means parents.
Nada mau = literally 'nothing bad'. For a feminine noun you'd hear má: Uma nota nada má.
Arrasei comes from arrasar, 'to flatten' — like saying 'I smashed it!'. Very popular with kids.
Portuguese schools mark 1 to 5 up to year 9, so cinco is top. Older students would say Tive vinte! (out of 20).
Passei = 'I passed', from passar. The one you don't want to say is Chumbei! — 'I failed'.
Fixe is Portugal's word for 'cool'; Brazilians say legal. Que + describing word = 'How ...!'
Diz is 'say!' to one person, from dizer. Add me for Diz-me = 'Tell me'.
Obrigada literally means 'obliged'. A girl says obrigada, a boy says obrigado.
Literally 'How does one say it?' — what Portuguese parents ask when a kid forgets the magic words.
De nada = 'of nothing', i.e. it was nothing. You may also hear Não tem de quê.
Não faz mal = 'it does no harm'. It's the go-to reply when someone says sorry.
Santinho ('little saint') is what people in Portugal say after a sneeze. Some say Saúde! ('Health!').
Com licença = 'with permission' — for getting past or butting in politely. Desculpa is more for 'sorry'.

phrases.pt: Bate à porta antes de entrares.
phrases.ph: baht ah POR-tuh AHN-tush duh ayn-TRAH-rush
phrases.note: Entrares: Portuguese can add -es to entrar to show 'you' are the one doing it. A very Portuguese trick.
Falta de educação = 'lack of manners'. Educação often means manners and upbringing, not just schooling.
Querida ('dear') is for a girl, querido for a boy. Dad would say obrigado — that word follows the speaker.
After não, the verb ending changes: interrompe (interrupt!) becomes não interrompas (don't interrupt).
Pedir desculpa = 'to ask for forgiveness', the normal way to say sorry. Ao = a + o ('to the').

phrases.en: Say it like you mean it.
phrases.note: A sério = 'seriously, for real'. On its own, A sério? means 'Really?'

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.pt: Não fales com a boca cheia.
phrases.ph: nown FAH-luhsh kohn uh BOH-kuh SHAY-uh
phrases.note: Cheia = 'full', ending in -a to match a boca. Não fales = 'don't talk' to one person.

phrases.en: Don't speak to me like that.
phrases.note: Me ('to me') comes before fales because of não. Assim = 'like that'.
Cuidado com ... = 'Careful with ...'. It works for anything: Cuidado com o cão!
Avó (grandma) has a sloping accent; avô (grandpa) has a little hat. One mark changes the person!
Maneiras = 'manners'. Literally 'What manners are those?' — a telling-off, not a real question.
Por favor = 'for (a) favour'. It can go at the end too: Passa-me o sal, por favor.
Obrigada means 'obliged', so it matches whoever is thanking: girls say obrigada, boys obrigado.
Muito = 'very/much'. Want to go further? Muitíssimo obrigada! A boy says obrigado.
Desculpa is 'sorry' to someone you call tu. To a teacher or a stranger, say Desculpe.

phrases.en: Excuse me, can I get past?
phrases.note: Posso ...? = 'Can I ...?' Swap in any verb: Posso ir? Posso comer?
Pelo = por + o ('for the'). Jantar is dinner; almoço is lunch.
Adoro-te: te ('you') goes after the verb with a hyphen. Amo-te sounds more romantic, so families often say Adoro-te.
Também ('too') at the start pulls te in front of the verb — not adoro-te também.
Não há problema = 'there's no problem'. Há means 'there is' or 'there are'.
Está bem? = 'OK?'. In quick speech it often shrinks to Tá bem?
Já means 'already' — here it adds annoyance, like 'I've ALREADY said sorry!'

phrases.en: Sorry, can I just say something?
phrases.pt: Desculpa, posso só dizer uma coisa?
phrases.ph: dush-KOOL-puh, PO-soo so dee-ZAIR OO-muh KOY-zuh
phrases.note: Só = 'just/only'. Uma coisa ('a thing') is the everyday way to say 'something' here.
Bater à porta = 'to knock on the door'. Without à porta, Bate! on its own sounds like 'Hit!'

phrases.en: Sorry, I didn't do it on purpose.
phrases.note: De propósito = 'on purpose'. Portuguese says 'it wasn't on purpose' (não foi) rather than 'I didn't do it'.
Interrompeste = 'you interrupted', and -me ('me') is tacked on with a hyphen.
Boleia is Portugal's word for a lift; Brazilians say carona. Pela = por + a ('for the').

phrases.en: Can I leave the table, please?
phrases.pt: Posso levantar-me da mesa, por favor?
phrases.ph: PO-soo luh-vuhn-TAR-muh duh MAY-zuh, poor fuh-VOR
phrases.note: Levantar-me = 'get (myself) up'. The me goes after the verb with a hyphen; da = de + a ('from the').

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.note: Dás-me ...? = 'Will you give me ...?' — a friendly way to ask. The me ('me') sits after the verb with a hyphen.
As compras = 'the shopping'. Fazer compras means 'to go shopping'.
Segurar = 'to hold'. The me here means 'for me' — hold the door for me.
Ir abrir = 'go and open'. Portuguese needs no 'and' between ir and the next verb.
Precisar de = 'to need'. In Portugal the de stays: Preciso de ti = I need you.
Literally 'Do you want me to help you?' — the usual Portuguese way to offer help.
Deixa = 'leave it'. Eu faço is literally 'I do', but Portuguese often uses it to mean 'I'll do it'.
Dá cá = 'give here' — short and a bit bossy. Cá is a very Portuguese word for 'here'.
Mostrar = 'to show'. Add what you want to see: Mostra-me isso = Show me that.
Apanhar means 'grab' or 'catch' — you also apanhar o autocarro (catch the bus). Me = 'for me'.
Passa-me ... = 'Pass me ...' — perfect at the table: Passa-me o sal.

phrases.pt: O que é que se passa?
phrases.ph: oo kee eh kuh suh PAH-suh
phrases.note: O que é que se passa? = 'What's going on?' Slipping é que into questions is very typical of Portugal.
Óculos (glasses) is always plural, so it's os meus óculos, never o meu.
Viste = 'did you see'. Portugal uses this simple past where English says 'have you seen'.
Pesquisar = 'to search' or 'look up', especially online. A pesquisa = the search.
Encontrá-lo: 'it' (o) becomes lo after a verb ending in -r, and the r drops off.

phrases.en: Can you set this up for me?
phrases.note: Configurar = 'to set up' a phone or app. Isto = 'this' (near me); isso = 'that' (near you).

phrases.en: I could do with some help here.
phrases.note: Dar jeito = 'to come in handy'. Ajudinha = 'a little help' — -inha makes things small and friendly.
Podes ...? = 'Can you ...?' The me hooks onto ajudar with a hyphen.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: Ajudas-me? uses the present tense as a quick request, like 'Will you help me?'. Com isto = 'with this'.

phrases.en: Can you do this for me?
phrases.note: Por mim = 'for me'; por ti = 'for you'. Mim and ti are the forms used after little words like por.
Consegues ...? = 'Can you manage to ...?' — best when something is hard, like a stiff jar.
Chegar usually means 'to arrive' but also 'to reach'. Lá = 'there'.
Arranjar = 'to fix' in Portugal (it can also mean 'to get'). Consertar means 'fix' too.
Ver = 'to see', but here it means 'have a look at'. For 'Look!' say Olha!

phrases.pt: Podes ver se isto está bem?
phrases.note: Ver se ... está bem = 'see if ... is right' — handy for getting your TPC checked.

phrases.pt: Como é que se faz isto?
phrases.ph: KOH-moo eh kuh suh fahz EESH-too
phrases.note: Se makes it general: 'How is this done?' Fazer = 'to do' or 'to make'.

phrases.pt: O que é que isto quer dizer?
phrases.ph: oo kee eh kee EESH-too kair dee-ZAIR
phrases.note: Querer dizer = 'to mean' (literally 'to want to say'). Significar works too.
Ficar = 'to stay', but also 'to belong' or 'be located': A escola fica perto = The school is nearby.
Ensinar means 'to teach', so this asks someone to show you how to do something.
Vir = 'to come'; cá = 'here'. The quick version is Anda cá! = Come here!
Nisto = em + isto ('on this'). Portuguese says 'hold on to this': Segura nisto!
Levar = 'take/carry' away from where you are; trazer = 'bring' towards you.

phrases.en: Can you get this for me?
phrases.note: Trazer = 'to bring'. Another one to try: Traz-me um copo de água = Bring me a glass of water.
Encontrar = 'to find', procurar = 'to look for'. You procurar first, then (hopefully) encontrar!
O = 'it', stuck on after the verb. For something feminine, like a caneta (pen), say Viste-a?

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.note: Dar uma mão = 'to give a hand', just like English. Podes ...? = Can you ...?
Encravado = 'jammed' — for zips, doors, printers. For a feminine thing: A porta está encravada.
Partido = 'broken' for things that snap or smash. A machine that stops working is avariado.
Estar a + verb = doing something right now. Brazilians would say não está funcionando.
Não consigo = 'I can't manage it'. It's about ability — não posso means 'I'm not allowed' or 'I can't (go)'.
Outra vez = 'again' (literally 'another time'). De novo means the same.
Magoar = 'to hurt'. The -me on the end means 'myself': 'I hurt myself'.
Portuguese says 'I cut myself on the finger'. Dedo is finger or toe — a toe is dedo do pé.
O teu = 'yours' for a masculine thing (o lápis); for a feminine one (a borracha) say a tua.

phrases.en: I don't know how it works.
phrases.note: Sei = 'I know', from saber. Não sei ('I don't know') is one of the most useful phrases there is.
Demasiado = 'too (much)'. Muito means 'very', so É muito pesado is a softer complaint.

phrases.pt: O dinheiro não cai do céu.
phrases.ph: oo dee-NYAY-roo nown kye doo SEH-oo
phrases.note: Portuguese parents say money doesn't 'fall from the sky' instead of growing on trees.

phrases.en: What do you need it for?
phrases.pt: Para que é que precisas disso?
phrases.ph: pruh kee eh kuh pruh-SEE-zush DEE-soo
phrases.note: Para que ...? = 'What ... for?'. Disso = de + isso ('of that').
Demais after a describing word = 'too'. Caríssimo means 'super expensive'.
Quanto custa? = 'How much does it cost?'. For more than one thing: Quanto custam?
Paga! = 'Pay!' to one person. Com o teu dinheiro = 'with your money'.

phrases.en: You've already spent your pocket money.
phrases.note: Semanada is weekly pocket money in Portugal (from semana, week); mesada is monthly.
Dou-te = 'I give you'. Portuguese often uses the present for promises. Metade = half.

phrases.en: Put it on your birthday list.
phrases.note: In Portugal your birthday is often os anos: Faço anos amanhã = It's my birthday tomorrow.
Vamos + verb = 'we're going to ...'. Put não in front for 'we're not going to'.
Trocos = small coins. Troco (singular) is the change a shop gives you back.
Deitar fora = 'to throw away'. You'll hear it a lot: Deita isso fora! = Throw that away!
Mandar = 'to send' (it can also mean 'to boss about'). Te comes first because of já.
Two nãos: the first means 'No', the second makes the verb negative ('you don't need').

phrases.en: What happened to your birthday money?
phrases.pt: O que fizeste ao dinheiro dos anos?
phrases.ph: oo kuh fee-ZESH-tuh ow dee-NYAY-roo doo-ZUH-noosh
phrases.note: Literally 'What did you do to the birthday money?' Fizeste = 'you did', from fazer.
Poupar = 'to save' money (or energy). Ter de = 'to have to' — Portugal prefers de over que.

phrases.en: Do I look like a bank?
phrases.note: Ter cara de = 'to look like' (literally 'have the face of'). Tens cara de sono = You look sleepy.
Putting não at the end makes it firm: 'This month — no.' The plural of mês is meses.

phrases.en: You'll have to pay me back.
phrases.pt: Tens de me devolver o dinheiro.
phrases.ph: taynsh duh muh duh-vol-VAIR oo dee-NYAY-roo
phrases.note: Devolver = 'to give back', a false friend — it doesn't mean 'devolve'. Tens de = 'you have to'.
Saldos = 'the sales' in Portugal; Brazilians say liquidação. Esperar por = 'to wait for'.

phrases.en: Do you think I'm made of money?
phrases.note: Achar = 'to think' (give an opinion), not just 'to find'. Mum would say milionária.
No word for 'some' needed — Dás-me dinheiro? is literally 'Will you give me money?'

phrases.en: Can you send me some money?
phrases.note: Mandar-me = 'send me'. Mandas-me dinheiro? is a shorter, friendlier way to ask the same.
There's no separate 'borrow' here: you ask 'Will you lend me?' using emprestar.
Devolvo-te = 'I'll give (it) back to you'. The te still goes after the verb, even with depois ('later') in front.
Comprar = 'to buy'. In a shop you might hear Mais alguma coisa? = Anything else?

phrases.en: Can you buy this for me?
phrases.note: Compras-me = 'Will you buy me ...?' Short and sweet — works best with a smile.
Encomendar = 'to order' online or a takeaway. In a café you pedir instead.
Cartão = a bank card. Careful: carta usually means a letter.
Quanto custa? = How much does it cost? For more than one thing, say Quanto custam?
Libras = pounds. Só means 'only' and sits just before the verb: só custa.
Em promoção = on offer. You'll see promoções on signs in Portuguese supermarkets.
Precisar always takes de: preciso de + isto joins up to make preciso disto.
Toda a gente = everyone in Portugal (literally 'all the people'); Brazilians say todo mundo.
Ir às compras = to go shopping. Podemos...? = Can we...? works for loads of requests.
Ao = a + o ('to the'). Centro means the town centre; in Lisbon people call downtown a Baixa.

phrases.en: Can you take me to the shops?
phrases.note: In levar-me, the me ('me') goes after the verb with a hyphen. Podes = can you, to one person.

phrases.en: I don't have any money left.
phrases.note: Já não = not any more, so já não tenho dinheiro = I've got no money left.

phrases.en: Can I have my pocket money?
phrases.note: A mesada is pocket money paid monthly (mês = month). If you get it every week, it's a semanada.
Poupar = to save money. Estou a + verb shows something you're doing these days — never estou poupando in Portugal.
Demasiado = too (much). Portuguese people use it a lot; Brazilians more often say caro demais.
Barato = cheap, the opposite of caro. For 'super cheap', try baratíssimo.

phrases.en: I want to buy her a present.
phrases.note: Prenda = present in Portugal (Brazilians say presente). Lhe means 'for her' here and hooks onto the verb with a hyphen.

phrases.en: Can I use my birthday money?
phrases.pt: Posso usar o dinheiro dos meus anos?
phrases.ph: PO-soo oo-ZAR oo dee-NYAY-roo doosh mayooz AH-noosh
phrases.note: Portuguese people often say os meus anos (literally 'my years') for 'my birthday'. Aniversário works too.
Gastei = I spent (from gastar). Tudo = everything, so it's simply 'I spent everything'.

phrases.en: Can you lend me ten pounds?
phrases.note: Emprestar = to lend. Emprestas-me...? = Will you lend me...? with the me after the verb.
A set phrase meaning 'it's worth it' (literally 'it's worth the pain'). Não vale a pena = it's not worth it.
O troco = the change you get back. Ficar com = to keep (literally 'to stay with').
Põe = put (an order, from pôr). O cinto is a belt; in the car it's short for o cinto de segurança.

phrases.pt: Para de dar pontapés no banco.
phrases.ph: PAH-ruh duh dar pohn-tuh-PEZH noo BAHN-koo
phrases.note: Para de + verb = stop doing something. Banco here is the car seat, not a bank!
O telemóvel = mobile phone in Portugal; Brazilians say celular. Guarda = put away.
Quase = nearly. Estamos a chegar = we're arriving — estar a + verb for what's happening now.
Falta pouco literally means 'little is missing' — the Portuguese way to say 'not long now'.

phrases.en: Go to the toilet before we leave.
phrases.pt: Vai à casa de banho antes de sairmos.
phrases.ph: vye ah KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo AHN-tsh duh suh-EER-moosh
phrases.note: A casa de banho = the toilet in Portugal; Brazilians say banheiro. Antes de sairmos = before we leave.
Façam is an order to more than one kid (vocês). To just one, say Faz menos barulho.
Estou a tentar = I'm trying right now. In concentrar-me, the me ('myself') hangs on the end with a hyphen.
After não, the me jumps in front of the verb: não me distraias, not não distraias-me.

phrases.en: Who's in charge of the music?
phrases.pt: Quem é que escolhe a música?
phrases.ph: kayn eh kuh sh-KOH-lyuh uh MOO-zee-kuh
phrases.note: Quem é que...? = Who...? The é que ('is it that') is optional but very common in spoken questions.
In Portugal música means a song as well as music. Outra vez = again.

phrases.pt: Pega nas tuas coisas, já chegámos.
phrases.ph: PEH-guh nuhsh TOO-uhsh KOY-zuhsh, zhah shuh-GAH-moosh
phrases.note: Chegámos with an accent = we've arrived; in Portugal the accent separates it from chegamos, 'we arrive'.
Esperar por = to wait for. Ti is the word for 'you' after little words like por, para and de.

phrases.en: Are you getting out or not?
phrases.note: Sais = you get out (from sair). Short and impatient, just like the English.
Portuguese says 'enter in the car': no = em + o ('in the'). Entra = get in.

phrases.en: Hurry up, I'm in the car.
phrases.note: Despacha-te = hurry up, a very Portuguese way to say it. The te ('yourself') sits after the verb.
Parem = stop, said to more than one kid (vocês). Aí atrás = back there, where you are.
'Don't' orders change the verb's ending: come (eat!) becomes não comas (don't eat).

phrases.en: If you feel sick, tell me.
phrases.note: Enjoada = feeling car-sick (a boy is enjoado). Avisa-me = let me know.
Pela = por + a ('through the'), so olha pela janela = look out of the window.
Deixo-te literally means 'I leave you'. Portuguese often uses the present for 'I'll' plans.
Baixa = turn down (from baixar, to lower). With a capital, a Baixa is Lisbon's downtown.
The classic back-seat question. Já here means 'yet' or 'already'.
Faltar = to be left or missing. Quanto falta? works for time or distance.
Demorar = to take (time). Vamos demorar = we're going to take — ir + verb for the future.
Para onde = where to. For where something is, just use onde: Onde estamos?

phrases.en: Can I sit in the front?
phrases.note: À frente = in the front. Posso...? = Can I...? is the go-to way to ask permission.

phrases.en: Can you turn the music up?
phrases.pt: Podes pôr a música mais alta?
phrases.ph: PO-dsh pohr uh MOO-zee-kuh myz AL-tuh
phrases.note: Mais alta = louder (literally 'higher'). Pôr has an accent to tell it apart from por ('for').
Baixar = to turn down or lower. The opposite is pôr mais alto.
Escolher = to choose. Swap the end: Posso escolher o filme? = Can I choose the film?
Sítio = place in Portugal (Brazilians say lugar). Nalgum = em + algum, 'in some'.

phrases.pt: Preciso de ir à casa de banho.
phrases.ph: pruh-SEE-zoo deer ah KAH-zuh duh BUH-nyoo
phrases.note: Preciso de + verb = I need to. In Portugal the de stays; Brazilians often drop it.
Literally 'I have hunger'. Portuguese uses ter (to have), not 'to be', for being hungry.
Sede = thirst, and it goes with tenho just like fome. It has nothing to do with 'seed'!
Cansada is for a girl — a boy says cansado. It's estou (not sou) because tiredness passes.
Tenho frio = I (a person) feel cold. For the weather, say Está frio.
Literally 'I have heat'. Avoid estou quente for this — it can sound like you mean something else.

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating on?
phrases.note: Ligar = to switch on (and also to phone). Desligar switches it off.

phrases.en: Can you turn the air conditioning on?
phrases.note: O ar condicionado = air conditioning, almost word for word. Ligar here means switch on.
A janela = the window. Flip it with fechar: Podes fechar a janela? = Can you close it?
With no a ('the') before it, casa means your own home: ir para casa = go home.
Enjoada = feeling sick, often from travel (a boy says enjoado). Enjoar has nothing to do with 'enjoy'!
Carregar = to charge a battery (it also means to press or carry). O carregador = the charger.

phrases.en: Can I put my headphones in?
phrases.note: Auscultadores = headphones in Portugal; Brazilians say fones de ouvido.

phrases.pt: Ele está a dar pontapés no meu banco.
phrases.ph: ayl sh-TAH uh dar pohn-tuh-PEZH noo mayoo BAHN-koo
phrases.note: Dar pontapés = to kick (literally 'give kicks'). Está a dar shows he's doing it right now.
Trânsito = traffic. Há = there is or there are — one tiny word for both.
Estamos comes from estar, the verb for where people and things are.

phrases.en: Can you pass me my bag?
phrases.note: A mochila = backpack or school bag. Passar-me = pass me, with the me joined by a hyphen.
In Portugal people put o or a before names: o Monty, a Sofia. Vem = is coming.
Olhar para = to look at. A estrada is the road; a rua is a street in town.
Portuguese talks about the sun being there: está sol = it's sunny. Sol = sun.
De rachar means 'to crack' — so cold things could split. A fun Portuguese way to say freezing.
Guarda-chuva = umbrella, literally 'guard-rain'. Leva = take it with you.
Imenso = loads of — a very Portuguese word (Brazilians would say muito). Vento = wind.
Protetor solar = sun cream (people also say creme solar). Põe = put on.
Mais logo = later today, a phrase you'll hear all the time in Portugal.
Agasalhar-se = to wrap up warm; um agasalho is a warm top. The te after the verb means 'yourself'.
Está calor = it's hot (weather). Hoje = today, and it often goes first.
Gelo = ice — don't confuse it with gelado, which is ice cream! Lá fora = outside.
Está a nevar = it's snowing right now (estar a + verb). Nevar comes from neve, snow.
Vem aí = is on its way (literally 'comes there'). Tempestade = storm.

phrases.en: Bring the washing in, it's raining.
phrases.pt: Apanha a roupa, está a chover.
phrases.note: Apanhar a roupa = bring the washing in (literally 'pick up the clothes'). Apanhar also means catch.
Casaco = coat. Teu = your, to one person; to several you'd say o vosso casaco.
Vestir = to put on clothes. Portuguese says 'put on the coat', not 'your coat'.

phrases.en: You're not going out like that, it's freezing.
phrases.pt: Assim não sais, está um frio de rachar.
phrases.ph: uh-SEEN nown sysh, sh-TAH oon FREE-oo duh rruh-SHAR
phrases.note: Assim = like that. Assim não sais is a firm 'you're not going out like that'.
Tirar = to take off. Molhados = wet, ending in -os to match os sapatos.

phrases.en: Shut the door, you're letting the cold in.
phrases.pt: Fecha a porta, que está a entrar frio.
phrases.ph: FAY-shuh uh POR-tuh, kuh sh-TAH uh ayn-TRAR FREE-oo
phrases.note: Que here means 'because' — very common in spoken Portuguese. Literally 'cold is coming in'.

phrases.en: It's only a bit of rain.
phrases.note: Pingos = drops, so this means 'it's only a few drops' — barely raining.
Bebe (drink!) looks the same as 'he drinks' — the situation tells you it's an order.
False friend: constipação means a cold in Portugal, not constipation! Apanhar = to catch.
Vai + verb talks about the near future: Vai chover? Vai nevar? = Is it going to snow?
O tempo means both 'weather' and 'time' — the context tells you which.
Preciso de = I need. No need for um here: preciso de casaco sounds natural.
Encharcada = soaked through, for a girl — a boy says encharcado.
Que + noun! = What a...! Try Que frio! or Que chuva! too.
Literally 'I'm dying of cold' — a dramatic way to say freezing, just like in English.

phrases.en: What's the weather going to be like tomorrow?
phrases.pt: Como vai estar o tempo amanhã?
phrases.ph: KOH-moo vye sh-TAR oo TAYN-poo uh-muh-NYAHN
phrases.note: Amanhã = tomorrow, but de manhã = in the morning. Easy to mix up!
Está um gelo = it's freezing (literally 'it's an ice'). Aqui dentro = in here.
Não vou + verb = I'm not going to. Sounds stubborn — which is the point.
Assar = to roast, like a chicken in the oven. Estou a assar = I'm roasting.
Portuguese says 'I have the shoes soaked'. Encharcados ends in -os to match os sapatos.

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating up?
phrases.pt: Podes pôr o aquecimento mais alto?
phrases.ph: PO-dsh pohr oo uh-keh-see-MAYN-too myz AL-too
phrases.note: Pôr mais alto = turn up; pôr mais baixo = turn down. O aquecimento = the heating.
Odeio = I hate (from odiar). Chuva = rain, and chover = to rain.

phrases.en: Can we go to the beach?
phrases.note: À = a + a ('to the'), shown by the grave accent. So ir à praia = go to the beach.
Neve = snow, and in most of Portugal it's a rare sight — so this gets said with excitement.
To say you're not cold, hungry or thirsty, just put não before tenho.

phrases.en: Can you put the air con on?
phrases.note: O ar is short for o ar condicionado, just like 'air con'. Ar on its own means air.

phrases.pt: Que seca, está a chover outra vez.
phrases.ph: kuh SAY-kuh, sh-TAH uh shoo-VAYR OH-truh vaysh
phrases.note: Que seca! = What a drag! Funny, because seca also means drought — the opposite of rain.

phrases.pt: Agora tenho o cabelo todo despenteado.
phrases.ph: uh-GO-ruh TUH-nyoo oo kuh-BAY-loo TOH-doo dsh-payn-TYAH-doo
phrases.note: Despenteado = messy (pente = comb, so 'uncombed'). It matches o cabelo, so boys and girls both say it.

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift? It's pouring.
phrases.pt: Podes levar-me? Está a chover a potes.
phrases.ph: PO-dsh luh-VAR-muh sh-TAH uh shoo-VAYR uh potsh
phrases.note: A chover a potes = raining by the potful — Portugal's version of 'pouring'.

phrases.en: What do you want to do this weekend?
phrases.pt: O que queres fazer este fim de semana?
phrases.ph: oo kuh KEH-rsh fuh-ZAYR aysht feen duh suh-MUH-nuh
phrases.note: Queres = you want (the tu form of querer). Fim de semana = weekend, literally 'end of week'.
Jogar = to play games or sport. For instruments, Portuguese uses tocar.
Dar um passeio = go for a walk (literally 'give a walk'). Vamos here means 'let's'.

phrases.en: Shall we watch a film tonight?
phrases.note: A 'we' verb asked as a question (Vemos...?) is how you say 'Shall we...?'

phrases.pt: Hoje à noite vamos pedir pizza.
phrases.ph: ohzh ah noyt VUH-moosh puh-DEER PEET-suh
phrases.note: Pedir = to order food (and also to ask for). Hoje à noite = tonight.

phrases.en: We're going to Grandma's on Sunday.
phrases.pt: No domingo vamos a casa da avó.
phrases.ph: noo doo-MEEN-goo VUH-mooz uh KAH-zuh duh uh-VO
phrases.note: Watch the accent: avó = grandma, avô = grandad. A casa da avó = to grandma's.

phrases.en: Do you want to come with us?
phrases.note: Connosco = with us. That's the Portugal spelling; Brazilians write conosco.
Pressa = hurry. Não há pressa = there's no rush; estou com pressa = I'm in a hurry.
Está a ganhar = is winning right now. In Portugal it's always estar a + verb, never ganhando.
A tua vez = your turn; a minha vez = my turn. Handy for any board game.
Sair = to go out or leave. Vamos sair = we're going out.
Calçar = to put on shoes or socks — a verb just for footwear. Tirar takes them off.

phrases.pt: Agora é hora de estar em família.
phrases.ph: uh-GO-ruh eh O-ruh dsh-TAR ayn fuh-MEE-lyuh
phrases.note: É hora de... = it's time to... Estar em família = to be together as a family.
Visitar = to visit. The a is 'the': Portuguese says 'visit the grandma'.

phrases.en: Turn that off and come outside.
phrases.pt: Desliga isso e vem lá para fora.
phrases.ph: dzh-LEE-guh EE-soo ee vayn lah PAH-ruh FO-ruh
phrases.note: Desliga = switch off, the opposite of liga. Lá para fora = out there, outside.

phrases.en: You're coming whether you like it or not.
phrases.note: Quer queiras quer não = whether you like it or not — a set phrase parents love.

phrases.en: Some fresh air will do you good.
phrases.pt: Um pouco de ar fresco vai fazer-te bem.
phrases.ph: oon POH-koo dar FRAYSH-koo vye fuh-ZAYR-tuh bayn
phrases.note: Fazer-te bem = do you good. The te ('you') goes after fazer with a hyphen.

phrases.en: You can't spend all day in bed.
phrases.pt: Não podes passar o dia todo na cama.
phrases.ph: nown PO-dsh puh-SAR oo DEE-uh TOH-doo nuh KUH-muh
phrases.note: Não podes = you can't; podes is the tu ('you') form of poder, to be able. O dia todo = the whole day.
Meio-dia = midday, literally 'half-day'. Midnight is meia-noite. Já ('already') adds a bit of drama.

phrases.pt: Deixa de te queixar, vai ser divertido.
phrases.ph: DAY-shuh duh tuh kay-SHAR, vye sayr dee-vuhr-TEE-doo
phrases.note: Deixa de ... = stop doing ... (literally 'leave off'). Queixar-se is 'to moan'; the te means 'yourself'.
Anima-te: the te ('yourself') goes after the verb with a hyphen — literally 'liven yourself up'.

phrases.pt: Estás aborrecida? Então arruma o teu quarto.
phrases.ph: sh-TAHZ uh-boo-rruh-SEE-duh ayn-TOWN uh-RROO-muh oo tayoo KWAR-too
phrases.note: Aborrecida (bored) is for a girl; a boy is aborrecido. Arrumar = to tidy — you'll hear it about every mess.

phrases.pt: O que é que vamos ver?
phrases.ph: oo kee eh kuh VUH-moozh vayr
phrases.note: O que é que...? is the everyday Portuguese way to ask 'what...?' — the é que bit just makes it sound natural.
Podemos...? = Can we...? Swap in any verb: Podemos sair? (Can we go out?)

phrases.pt: Podemos ir a casa da avó?
phrases.ph: poo-DAY-mooz eer uh KAH-zuh duh uh-VO
phrases.note: Avó (with a sloping accent) is Grandma; avô (with a little hat) is Grandad. A casa da avó = to Grandma's house.
Pipocas = popcorn, always plural in Portugal. Just asking 'Fazemos...?' ('Do we make...?') is a friendly 'Shall we...?'

phrases.en: I don't want to watch that.
phrases.note: Isso = that (near you); isto = this (near me). Não goes straight before the verb to make it negative.
Posso...? = Can I...? — one of the most useful ways to start a question. Escolher = to choose.

phrases.en: Can we go to the cinema?
phrases.note: Ao is a + o squashed together, meaning 'to the'. So ao cinema = to the cinema, à praia = to the beach.
Batota is cheating at games in Portugal; Brazilians say trapaça. Estás a fazer = you're doing it right now.

phrases.en: What are we doing this weekend?
phrases.pt: O que é que vamos fazer este fim de semana?
phrases.ph: oo kee eh kuh VUH-moosh fuh-ZAYR aysht feen duh suh-MUH-nuh
phrases.note: Fim de semana = weekend, literally 'end of week'. Vamos + verb talks about plans: vamos fazer = we're going to do.
A girl says aborrecida, a boy aborrecido. Portuguese kids also groan 'Que seca!' (What a drag!).
Há = there is/there are. Portuguese happily doubles up negatives: não há nada is literally 'there isn't nothing'.

phrases.pt: Posso ficar a dormir até mais tarde?
phrases.ph: PO-soo fee-KAR uh door-MEER uh-TEH mysh tard
phrases.note: There's no single word for a lie-in, so you ask to 'stay sleeping until later': ficar a dormir até mais tarde.
Ficar = to stay. Na is em + a joined up ('in the'), so na cama = in bed.
Tenho de + verb = I have to. Portuguese says ir ('go') here, because you're going somewhere, not coming.
Alguma coisa = something (literally 'some thing'). Coisa is a feminine word, so it's divertida, not divertido.

phrases.en: I don't want to go for a walk.
phrases.pt: Não quero ir dar um passeio.
phrases.ph: nown KEH-roo eer dar oon puh-SAY-oo
phrases.note: Dar um passeio = to go for a walk — literally 'to give a walk'. The one-word verb passear means the same.
Já = already, so this is 'I've already got plans' — a handy way to wriggle out of things.

phrases.pt: Posso estar com as minhas amigas?
phrases.ph: PO-soo sh-TAR kohn uhzh MEE-nyuhz uh-MEE-guhsh
phrases.note: As minhas amigas = my (girl) friends. For boys or a mixed group, say os meus amigos. Estar com = to be with or see.
Uma seca = a drag — literally 'a drought'! Que seca! (What a bore!) is a very Portuguese moan.

phrases.en: It's the weekend, leave me alone.
phrases.pt: É fim de semana, deixem-me em paz.
phrases.ph: eh feen duh suh-MUH-nuh, DAY-shayn-muh ayn pash
phrases.note: Deixem-me speaks to both parents (vocês). To one person it's deixa-me em paz. Blunt — only for family.
Mandar vir = to have something brought to you — the usual Portuguese way to say 'get a takeaway'.
Em casa = at home, with no word for 'the'. Going home is ir para casa.
Parabéns means 'congratulations', and it's what people in Portugal say on your birthday. Feliz aniversário sounds more formal.

phrases.en: What do you want for your birthday?
phrases.pt: O que é que queres para os teus anos?
phrases.ph: oo kee eh kuh KEH-rsh PAH-ruh oosh tayooz AH-noosh
phrases.note: Os teus anos = your birthday in everyday Portuguese (literally 'your years'). Aniversário is the dictionary word.
Pede comes from pedir (to ask for), so you literally 'ask for a wish'. Desejo = wish.
Soprar = to blow. Velas are candles — and also the sails on a boat.
Natal = Christmas; it comes from the word for birth. The big Christmas Eve family dinner in Portugal is called a Consoada.
Ano Novo = New Year, with novo (new) after the noun, as most describing words are. New Year's Eve is a passagem de ano.
Festa = party. Portuguese 'does' a party: fazer uma festa, rather than 'having' one.

phrases.en: Who do you want to invite?
phrases.note: Convidar = to invite, and the invitation itself is um convite. Quem = who.
Assinaste = you signed. Portuguese uses this simple past where English says 'have you...?', often with já (already).
Presentes = presents — an easy one. Abre is the 'do it!' form of abrir (to open) for one person.

phrases.en: I can't believe you're fifteen already!
phrases.pt: Nem acredito que já tens quinze anos!
phrases.ph: nayn uh-kruh-DEE-too kuh zhah taynsh keenz AH-noosh
phrases.note: Portuguese says you 'have' years: tens quinze anos. Nem acredito = I can't even believe it.
In Portugal the birthday song is simply called os parabéns. Vamos + verb = let's...
The classic nudge to say thank you. Se diz = 'one says', so it's literally 'How does one say it?'
A girl says obrigada, a boy obrigado — it matches the person saying thanks. À = a + a, 'to the'.
Abras is the special 'don't' form of abrir. The o ('it') jumps in front of the verb because of não.

phrases.en: Don't invite too many people, OK?
phrases.pt: Não convides muita gente, está bem?
phrases.ph: nown kohn-VEE-dsh MOOYN-tuh zhent, sh-TAH bayn
phrases.note: Está bem? = OK? — often squashed to 'tá bem?'. Gente = people, and it's always singular: muita gente.
Às onze = at eleven. Times take às because the hidden word horas (hours) is feminine; one o'clock is à uma.

phrases.en: Who's going to clear all this up?
phrases.pt: Quem é que vai arrumar isto tudo?
phrases.ph: kayn eh kuh vye uh-rroo-MAR EESH-too TOO-doo
phrases.note: Isto tudo = all this. Arrumar means to tidy or clear up — a word you'll hear constantly at home.

phrases.en: Go and get changed, the guests are coming.
phrases.pt: Vai mudar de roupa, que os convidados estão a chegar.
phrases.ph: vye moo-DAR duh RROH-puh, kuh oosh kohn-vee-DAH-doosh sh-TOWN uh shuh-GAR
phrases.note: Mudar de roupa = to change clothes. Estão a chegar = they're arriving right now (estar a + verb).

phrases.en: Don't eat all the crisps before they get here.
phrases.pt: Não comas as batatas fritas todas antes de eles chegarem.
phrases.ph: nown KOH-muhz uhzh buh-TAH-tuhsh FREE-tuhsh TOH-duhz AHN-tsh DAY-lsh shuh-GAH-rayn
phrases.note: Batatas fritas means both crisps and chips in Portugal. Chegarem is chegar with an ending showing 'they' are arriving.
Fazer means both 'do' and 'make', so it turns up everywhere — including fazer uma festa, to have a party.
Os meus presentes = my presents. Portuguese usually keeps 'the' before 'my': o meu, a minha, os meus.

phrases.en: I'd like new trainers for my birthday.
phrases.pt: Queria umas sapatilhas novas para os meus anos.
phrases.ph: kuh-REE-uh OO-muhsh suh-puh-TEE-lyuhzh NO-vuhsh PAH-ruh oozh mayooz AH-noosh
phrases.note: Sapatilhas = trainers in Portugal; Brazilians say tênis. Queria ('I'd like') is the polite way to ask.

phrases.en: When are we putting the tree up?
phrases.pt: Quando é que montamos a árvore?
phrases.ph: KWAHN-doo eh kuh mohn-TUH-mooz uh AR-voor
phrases.note: Montar = to put up or build. The Christmas tree is a árvore de Natal.

phrases.pt: Quantos dias faltam para o Natal?
phrases.ph: KWAHN-toozh DEE-uhsh FAL-town PAH-ruh oo nuh-TAL
phrases.note: Faltar = to be missing or left, so this is literally 'How many days are missing until Christmas?'
Bolo = cake. Há means both 'there is' and 'is there?' — your voice makes it a question.
Pelos = por + os, 'for the'. A girl says obrigada; a boy says obrigado.

phrases.pt: O que é que me deram?
phrases.ph: oo kee eh kuh muh DEH-rown
phrases.note: Deram is the 'you lot' form of dar (to give), speaking to both parents. The me sits before the verb after a question word.
Adoro = I love it — Portuguese doesn't need the 'it'. Works for presents, food and films.

phrases.en: It's not what I asked for.
phrases.pt: Não é o que eu pedi.
phrases.ph: nown eh oo kuh ayoo puh-DEE
phrases.note: Pedi = I asked for, from pedir. Don't mix it up with perguntar, which is asking a question.
In Portugal you put 'the' before names of people you know: a Lúcia, o Monty. Lúcia is the Portuguese spelling.

phrases.pt: Quando é a minha festa de anos?
phrases.ph: KWAHN-doo eh uh MEE-nyuh FESH-tuh DAH-noosh
phrases.note: Festa de anos = birthday party, the everyday way to say it in Portugal. Festa de aniversário is fine too.
Enfeitar = to decorate for a party or Christmas; the decorations are os enfeites.
Entusiasmada = excited (a boy says entusiasmado). Avoid excitada — it has a rude-ish meaning!
Mal posso esperar = I can hardly wait. Here mal means 'hardly', not 'badly'.
Fazer anos = to have a birthday, literally 'to make years'. You'll hear it far more than aniversário.
Cantem is the 'don't' form for vocês (you lot), aimed at the whole family. To one person: não cantes.
Passar vergonha = to feel embarrassed. The me ('me') joins the end of fazem with a hyphen.

phrases.pt: As minhas amigas podem dormir cá em casa?
phrases.ph: uhzh MEE-nyuhz uh-MEE-guhsh PO-dayn door-MEER kah ayn KAH-zuh
phrases.note: Cá em casa = here at ours; cá ('here') is very European Portuguese. For boys: os meus amigos.

phrases.en: Can you stay upstairs during the party?
phrases.pt: Podem ficar lá em cima durante a festa?
phrases.ph: PO-dayn fee-KAR lah ayn SEE-muh doo-RAHN-tuh FESH-tuh
phrases.note: Lá em cima = upstairs, literally 'up there'; downstairs is lá em baixo. Podem = can you (lot)?
Cansada is for a girl; ask a boy Estás cansado? Estás comes from estar, used for how you feel right now.

phrases.en: What time are you going to bed?
phrases.pt: A que horas é que vais para a cama?
phrases.ph: uh kee O-ruhz eh kuh vysh PAH-ruh KUH-muh
phrases.note: A que horas...? = At what time...? Portuguese asks about the 'hours' (horas).

phrases.en: You need to go to bed.
phrases.pt: Tens de ir para a cama.
phrases.note: Tens de + verb = you have to... Swap the ending for other orders: Tens de comer, Tens de estudar.
Está a ficar = it's getting — estar a + verb shows it's happening now. Brazilians would say está ficando.
Amanhã = tomorrow, but de manhã = in the morning. They look alike, so watch out!

phrases.en: Go and get ready for bed.
phrases.note: Preparar-te: the te ('yourself') sticks to the end of the verb with a hyphen. Vai + verb = go and...
Portuguese 'washes' teeth: lavar os dentes. It says 'the teeth', not 'your teeth', because it's obvious whose.
Lavaste = you washed. Starting with já turns it into 'Have you... yet?' — useful for checking on anything.
Telemóvel is a phone in Portugal; Brazilians say celular. Largar = to let go of — quite a firm way to say it.
Põe is the 'do it!' form of pôr (to put). A carregar = charging, and the charger is o carregador.
Apagar = to switch off; acender = to switch on. Portuguese just says 'the light', not 'your light'.

phrases.pt: Não fiques acordada até muito tarde.
phrases.ph: nown FEE-kuhz uh-koor-DAH-duh uh-TEH MOOYN-too tard
phrases.note: Acordada = awake, for a girl; a boy is acordado. Fiques is the 'don't' form of ficar (to stay).
Ainda = still (or yet). A boy would be asked Ainda estás acordado?

phrases.pt: Porque é que ainda estás acordada?
phrases.ph: POOR-kee eh kee uh-EEN-duh sh-TAHZ uh-koor-DAH-duh
phrases.note: Porque é que...? = Why...? In Portugal it's written as one word, porque; Brazilians write por que in questions.
Literally 'go sleep' — Portuguese doesn't need an 'and' or 'to' between vai and the next verb.
Boa noite is singular in Portuguese, unlike Spanish buenas noches. It also means 'good evening'.
Dorme is the 'do it!' form of dormir (to sleep) for one person. Bem = well.
Até amanhã = until tomorrow. Até + a time works for lots of goodbyes: até logo = see you later.

phrases.en: Did you have a good day?
phrases.note: Correr means 'to run', but correr bem means 'to go well' — so literally 'Did your day run well?'
Vestir = to put on clothes. O pijama is singular in Portuguese, even though English says pyjamas.
Mete-te = put yourself; the te goes after the verb with a hyphen. Na cama = in bed.
O despertador = the alarm clock, from despertar (to wake up). Puseste = you put, from the awkward verb pôr.

phrases.pt: Deixa o telemóvel lá em baixo.
phrases.ph: DAY-shuh oo tuh-luh-MO-vel lah ayn BY-shoo
phrases.note: Lá em baixo = downstairs, literally 'down there'. In Portugal em baixo is written as two words.

phrases.pt: Dez minutos e depois apagas a luz.
phrases.ph: dezh mee-NOO-tooz ee duh-POYZ uh-PAH-guhz uh loosh
phrases.note: Apagas = you switch off. Using the plain 'you do' form sounds like a firm plan, like 'then you turn it off'.
Tudo = everything. Pronto (ready) matches tudo, so it stays pronto even when talking to a girl.

phrases.en: Do you want a hot chocolate?
phrases.note: Chocolate quente = hot chocolate, with the describing word after the noun. Quente = hot; frio = cold.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, people are sleeping.
phrases.pt: Faz menos barulho, que está gente a dormir.
phrases.ph: fahzh MAY-noosh buh-ROO-lyoo, kuh sh-TAH ZHAYN-tuh door-MEER
phrases.note: Barulho = noise. Está gente a dormir = there are people sleeping — gente takes a singular verb.
Bons sonhos = good dreams. Some Portuguese parents say sonhos cor-de-rosa — pink dreams!
Adoro-te = love you, with te after the verb. Amo-te is stronger and more romantic; families say adoro-te a lot.
A girl says cansada; a boy says cansado. For 'really, really tired', try cansadíssima.
Vou = I'm going, from ir. You go para a cama — literally 'towards the bed'.
Just put não before the verb to say 'not'. A boy says Não estou cansado.

phrases.en: I'm not going to bed yet.
phrases.pt: Ainda não vou para a cama.
phrases.note: Ainda não = not yet. It comes before the verb — the opposite end of the sentence from English.
Não é assim tão... = it's not that... A handy way to play things down: não é assim tão difícil.
Só = just/only. Portuguese puts mais (more) before the number: mais cinco minutos.
Estou a acabar = I'm finishing right now (estar a + verb). Só slots into the middle to mean 'just'.
Tomar banho = to have a shower or bath — literally 'take a bath'. It's where casa de banho (bathroom) comes from.
Carregador comes from carregar, to charge (or carry). Onde está...? = Where is...?
Viste = you saw, from ver. Portuguese asks 'did you see?' where English says 'have you seen?'

phrases.en: Can you turn the light off?
phrases.note: Podes...? = Can you...? to one family member. Add por favor to sound nicer.
Fechar = to shut; abrir = to open. Blunt without por favor — fine with family, rude to anyone else.
Aberta = open, ending in -a to match a porta, a feminine word. Deixar = to leave something as it is.
Say boa noite at bedtime and from the evening on. Earlier it's boa tarde (good afternoon) or bom dia (good morning).
Até = until, amanhã = tomorrow. You'll hear Até amanhã! at the school gate too.
Não consigo = I can't (manage to). If you're not allowed to do something, that's não posso instead.
Pesadelo = nightmare — it's related to pesado, heavy. Tive = I had, from ter.

phrases.en: Can you wake me up at seven?
phrases.note: Acordar-me: the me is joined to the end of the verb with a hyphen. Acordar = to wake someone (or yourself) up.
Pus = I put, a short, odd past form of pôr. Já adds 'already', like 'I've already set it'.
Descansar = to rest. Descansa bem ('rest well') is a warm way to wish someone a good night.

phrases.en: Can I read for a bit?
phrases.note: Um bocadinho = a little bit — really common in Portugal, where Brazilians would say um pouquinho.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.pt: O Monty pode dormir no meu quarto?
phrases.ph: oo MON-tee pod door-MEER noo mayoo KWAR-too
phrases.note: Quarto = bedroom (it also means 'a quarter'). Notice o Monty — Portuguese puts 'the' before names.

phrases.en: I'm cold, can I have another blanket?
phrases.pt: Estou com frio, dás-me outro cobertor?
phrases.ph: sh-TOH kohn FREE-oo, DAHZH-muh OH-troo koo-buhr-TOR
phrases.note: Estou com frio = I'm cold (literally 'I'm with cold'). Dás-me...? = Will you give me...?

phrases.en: What time do I have to get up?
phrases.pt: A que horas é que tenho de me levantar?
phrases.ph: uh kee O-ruhz eh kuh TUH-nyoo duh muh luh-vuhn-TAR
phrases.note: Levantar-se = to get up. After tenho de, the me can sit before the verb: tenho de me levantar.
